shard.title: The Middle East and the Indian Ocean
shard.author: regional historian: Middle East and Indian Ocean
shard.note: Covers Arabia, the Gulf, the Fertile Crescent mandates, the two British occupations of the Levant and Constantinople, informal empire in Iran, and the Indian Ocean islands from Mauritius to the Chagos. Territories in the Indian Ocean carry region "indian-ocean" and so differ from the shard region; that is deliberate. Cyprus belongs to the Mediterranean shard and Egypt and Sudan to the Nile shard; the 1875 Suez Canal share purchase is recorded here as an event because it explains why Britain held Aden and the Gulf.

territories.name: Aden
territories.formalName: Colony of Aden (from 1963 the State of Aden)

namesOverTime.name: Aden Settlement
namesOverTime.note: A 'settlement' of the Bombay Presidency, like Karachi or Sind: an Indian possession, not a colony of the Colonial Office.

namesOverTime.name: State of Aden
namesOverTime.note: The colony's name inside the Federation of South Arabia. Aden's voters were never asked whether they wanted to join it.

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: Independent as the People's Republic of South Yemen in 1967, Marxist-Leninist as the PDRY from 1970, united with North Yemen in 1990. Aden is Yemen's declared economic capital.

geoCoverage.label: The peninsula, the crater and the harbour
geoCoverage.change: Aden began as roughly 190 square kilometres of volcanic rock around one of the finest natural harbours on earth. Britain added Little Aden and the mainland hinterland strip in 1868 and 1937; the drawn shape here is the wider 1937 colony.

acquisitions.how: Royal Navy ships shelled Aden and about 700 Royal Marines and Bombay European and Indian troops stormed the town, killing roughly 130 of its defenders and taking it from Sultan Muhsin bin Fadl of Lahej.

counterparties.name: Sultan Muhsin bin Fadl al-Abdali of Lahej
counterparties.lost: He lost Aden's harbour and its customs revenue, the town's 600-odd inhabitants, and the right to tax the trade of the whole Gulf of Aden coast; his family received a small annual stipend instead.

counterparties.name: The people of Aden town
counterparties.lost: A fishing and pilgrim town of about 600 people became a garrison and coal depot; within twenty years its population was over 20,000, most of them newcomers under military rule.

instrument.name: Treaty of 1839 with the Sultan of Lahej, imposed after the assault
instrument.note: The pretext was the plundering of the wrecked Indian ship Deria Dowlat in 1837. Captain Stafford Bettesworth Haines had first negotiated a purchase; when the Sultan's son repudiated it, Haines took the town by force.

people.name: Stafford Bettesworth Haines
people.role: Indian Navy commander who surveyed, negotiated for, then seized Aden and governed it for 15 years

people.name: Sultan Muhsin bin Fadl al-Abdali
people.role: ruler of Lahej who lost Aden and attacked it three times in the two years afterwards

cost.note: About 130 of Aden's defenders were killed for the loss of 15 British and Indian troops; the figures come from Haines's own dispatches and no independent count exists.

warrant.author: Captain Stafford Bettesworth Haines, in his own despatches
warrant.work: Haines’s despatches on the storming of Aden
warrant.supports: About 130 of Aden's defenders were killed for the loss of 15 British and Indian troops; the figures come from Haines's own dispatches and no independent count exists.
warrant.check: East India Company and Government of India military returns are in the India Office Records at the British Library (IOR series) and in the WO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

acquisitions.resistance: Lahej forces counter-attacked Aden in November 1839, May 1840 and July 1840; the last assault put roughly 5,000 men against the garrison and failed against artillery.

evidence.author: Robert J. Blyth
evidence.work: The Empire of the Raj: India, Eastern Africa and the Middle East, 1858-1947
evidence.supports: Aden's capture and its administration as an Indian, not a Colonial Office, possession.

statusPeriods.label: Held by the East India Company from Bombay
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Aden was taken by the East India Company, paid for out of Indian revenue and governed by a Political Resident answering to the Governor of Bombay. No British minister in London ordered its capture.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody in Aden voted for anything. The Resident ruled by executive order under martial-law powers.
statusPeriods.note: Haines was recalled in 1854 and imprisoned for debt in Bombay over missing Aden accounts; he died before his trial ended.

statusPeriods.label: A district of the Bombay Presidency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: When the Crown took over the Company in 1858 Aden passed with it, and for 74 years an Arabian port was administered as a district of western India, its laws Indian, its currency the rupee, its police and clerks recruited in Bombay.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Aden had no elected body of any kind until 1955.
statusPeriods.note: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and turned Aden into one of the busiest coaling stations in the world; by 1900 it bunkered over a thousand steamers a year.

statusPeriods.label: Chief Commissioner's Province of India
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Bombay handed Aden to the Government of India directly, so for five years Aden was a province of India governed from Delhi and Simla.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Crown Colony under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: India was moving towards self-government, so Britain cut Aden out of it and made it a Crown Colony run by a Governor answering to the Colonial Office in London. Aden left the empire's Indian half and joined its African and Arabian half on the same day Burma did.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Aden, under the Colonial Office, London
statusPeriods.franchise: The first Legislative Council elections were held in 1955 on a franchise restricted to men born in the colony: about 5,000 voters out of a population near 140,000. Most of Aden's workforce were migrants from the Protectorate or Yemen and could never qualify.
statusPeriods.note: BP's refinery at Little Aden opened in 1954 after the loss of Abadan in Iran; by the early 1960s Aden was the second-busiest bunkering port in the world after New York.

statusPeriods.label: State of Aden inside the Federation of South Arabia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain merged the port into a federation of the sultanates it had built inland, over the objections of Aden's trade unions and without a referendum. The Governor became a High Commissioner; from October 1963 he governed under emergency powers.
statusPeriods.franchise: Aden's legislature was suspended under the emergency. The federal assembly was appointed by rulers, not elected.
statusPeriods.note: The merger was designed to dilute Aden's radical, literate, unionised electorate inside a federation of conservative rulers. It did the opposite: it made the port the centre of the revolt.

departures.how: After four years of insurgency Britain abandoned the federation it had built, flew out the last 3,500 troops on 29 November 1967 and handed power to the National Liberation Front, which had already driven its rival FLOSY out of the streets.

led.name: Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi
led.role: secretary-general of the National Liberation Front; first president of South Yemen

led.name: Abdullah al-Asnag
led.role: trade unionist who built the Aden Trades Union Congress and led the People's Socialist Party, then FLOSY

led.name: Humphrey Trevelyan
led.role: last High Commissioner, sent in May 1967 to organise a withdrawal rather than a settlement

led.name: Colin Mitchell
led.role: commanded the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders who retook Crater in July 1967; the press called him 'Mad Mitch'

departures.movement: National Liberation Front (NLF); rival Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen (FLOSY)

cost.note: Estimates of the whole Aden Emergency vary widely. British service deaths are usually given as about 90 to 130 in Aden and Radfan; several hundred civilians were killed by bombs and shootings, and hundreds more died in the NLF-FLOSY fighting of 1967. No agreed total exists, and the local dead were never systematically counted.

departures.borders: The old colony boundary vanished: Aden and the protectorate sultanates became one state whose frontier with North Yemen was the Anglo-Ottoman 'Violet Line' of 1914, drawn by British and Turkish surveyors and still the reason Yemen argued with itself for decades.

instrument.name: Geneva talks between Britain and the NLF, 21-29 November 1967
instrument.note: There was no independence ceremony with the Union Flag lowered before a new prime minister. The last British troops left before the NLF took over.

evidence.author: Spencer Mawby
evidence.work: British Policy in Aden and the Protectorates 1955-67: Last Outpost of a Middle East Empire
evidence.supports: The Federation, the Emergency and the collapse of British policy in 1967.

violence.note: Britain fought the Radfan campaign in 1964 with air strikes and village demolitions, interned suspects at Al-Mansoura, and left after Amnesty International published allegations of torture in Aden's interrogation centres in 1966.

consequences.economicLegacy: Aden's economy was the harbour: bunkering, the BP refinery and a duty-free port serving ships between Europe and Asia. The Suez Canal closed in June 1967 and stayed shut for eight years, and Aden's traffic collapsed before independence was a week old.
consequences.borderLegacy: The line Britain and the Ottomans drew in 1914 became the border between South and North Yemen and the fault line of the 1972, 1979 and 1994 wars between them.

commonwealth.note: South Yemen never joined the Commonwealth. It is one of the very few former British possessions that did not.

peak.populationNote: The 1955 census counted 138,441 people in Aden Colony, of whom about 36,000 were Yemenis from beyond the border and 15,800 Indians. By 1963 the working population was near 225,000. Roughly half of Aden's workers had no vote because they had been born outside the colony.

evidence.author: Spencer Mawby
evidence.work: British Policy in Aden and the Protectorates 1955-67: Last Outpost of a Middle East Empire
evidence.supports: The last decade of British Aden.

evidence.author: Glen Balfour-Paul
evidence.work: The End of Empire in the Middle East: Britain's Relinquishment of Power in her Last Three Arab Dependencies
evidence.supports: Aden, Kuwait and the Gulf as a single withdrawal story.

evidence.author: Robert J. Blyth
evidence.work: The Empire of the Raj: India, Eastern Africa and the Middle East, 1858-1947
evidence.supports: Aden governed from Bombay and Delhi until 1937.

pedagogy.hook: For 98 years Aden was governed as part of India. Its policemen came from Bombay, its money was the rupee, and London only took it over in 1937 because India was about to be given away.

misconception.belief: Britain ran its empire from London, through the Colonial Office.
misconception.correction: Aden, the whole Persian Gulf, British Somaliland and for a time Zanzibar were run from India, on Indian money, by Indian Army officers. Historians call it a sub-empire. When India left in 1947 the Foreign Office had to invent a way to keep the Gulf, and had none of the machinery.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Aden shows what a naval empire was actually for. Britain wanted a coaling station on the road to India and took a town of 600 people to get it. When the road to India no longer led anywhere, the town became indefensible.

keyDates.what: Marines storm Aden; Britain's first colonial conquest of Victoria's reign
The Suez Canal opens and Aden becomes a world coaling port
Aden is cut out of India and made a Crown Colony
The Aden Emergency begins in the Radfan mountains
Britain leaves; the NLF proclaims South Yemen

territories.name: Aden Protectorate
territories.formalName: The Western and Eastern Aden Protectorates

namesOverTime.name: The Nine Cantons / the Aden hinterland
Aden Protectorate
namesOverTime.note: Split for administration into the Western Aden Protectorate, inland of Aden, and the Eastern Aden Protectorate, the Hadhramaut and Mahra.

namesOverTime.name: The southern governorates of Yemen
namesOverTime.note: Independent as South Yemen in 1967, united with the north in 1990, and the ground of a secession war in 1994 and a partition in all but name since 2015.

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: The protectorate states became the governorates of South Yemen in 1967 and of united Yemen in 1990. The Southern Movement has campaigned since 2007 for southern separation.

geoCoverage.label: About 90 sultanates, emirates and sheikhdoms
geoCoverage.change: Britain signed protection treaties one ruler at a time from 1886 to 1954. Between and beyond them lay desert and mountain nobody administered, which is why this shape is drawn hatched: British authority covered treaty relationships, not ground.

date.note: There was no single act. Britain signed protection treaties with rulers one at a time over nearly thirty years, beginning with the Mahra sultan in 1886 and the Aqrabi and Lower Yafa sheikhs in 1888.

acquisitions.how: British political officers signed protection treaties with about 30 rulers between 1886 and 1914, each promising a stipend and British protection in return for a bar on dealing with any other foreign power, chiefly to shut out the Ottomans and the French.

counterparties.name: The sultans, emirs and sheikhs of the Aden hinterland
counterparties.lost: They kept their thrones and their internal power but lost the right to make any agreement with an outside state, and became dependent on British subsidies paid from Aden.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Istanbul claimed sovereignty over the whole of Yemen and was pushed back to the line agreed in the Anglo-Ottoman Convention of 9 March 1914, giving up any claim south of it.

instrument.name: Protection treaties with individual rulers; boundary fixed by the Anglo-Ottoman Convention
instrument.note: The 1914 line, surveyed by a joint commission and drawn in violet pencil, is still called the Violet Line.

people.name: Sultan Ali bin Abdullah al-Afrar
people.role: Mahra ruler of Qishn and Socotra; signed the first protection treaty in 1886

acquisitions.resistance: The Zaydi imams of Sanaa never accepted the line and raided across it; Imam Yahya's forces occupied parts of the Western Protectorate in the 1920s until the RAF bombed them out and the Treaty of Sanaa of 1934 fixed a forty-year truce.

contested.note: There is no agreed start date for the Aden Protectorate. Some historians date it from the first stipendiary treaty with Lahej in 1839, some from 1886, some from the formal creation of a single 'Aden Protectorate' in 1937. This record uses 1886 and says so.

evidence.author: R. J. Gavin
evidence.work: Aden Under British Rule, 1839-1967
evidence.supports: The treaty system and the extension of protection inland.

date.note: The advisory treaties were signed one state at a time over seventeen years; the Qu'aiti state of Mukalla signed first, in 1937.

acquisitions.how: Britain replaced protection with 'advice': under the new advisory treaties a ruler had to accept a British adviser and take his advice on everything except religion and custom, which turned nominal protection into real administration.

counterparties.name: The Qu'aiti and Kathiri sultans of the Hadhramaut and the Western Protectorate rulers
counterparties.lost: They lost control of their own budgets, courts, armed forces and appointments to a resident British adviser, while keeping their titles and their stipends.

instrument.name: Advisory treaties, beginning with the Qu'aiti Sultanate of Shihr and Mukalla

people.name: Harold Ingrams
people.role: Resident Adviser in the Hadhramaut; got some 1,400 warring lineages to sign the three-year truce called Ingrams' Peace in 1937

people.name: Doreen Ingrams
people.role: travelled and negotiated the truce with her husband and wrote the survey of the Hadhramaut that Britain governed by

people.name: Sultan Salih bin Ghalib al-Qu'aiti
people.role: Qu'aiti ruler of Mukalla; the first to sign an advisory treaty

acquisitions.resistance: Hadhrami nationalists and returning migrants from Java and Singapore built parties in the 1950s; from 1963 the National Liberation Front simply abolished the sultanates.

evidence.author: Harold Ingrams
evidence.work: Arabia and the Isles
evidence.supports: The Hadhramaut truce and the working of the advisory system, by the man who ran it.

statusPeriods.label: Treaties, stipends and almost no administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain paid stipends and promised protection, and in return the rulers dealt with no one else. Political officers in Aden rarely travelled inland; the RAF bombed villages from 1919 when a ruler defied them, which was cheaper than governing.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the usual 3 for a protectorate: until the 1930s Britain had no administration inland at all, collected no tax, ran no courts and enforced its will chiefly by air.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Aden, under the Government of India
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The rulers were hereditary and the British officers were appointed.

statusPeriods.label: Western and Eastern Aden Protectorates, run by advisers
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British Residents at Mukalla and Aden placed an adviser beside each ruler whose advice had to be taken. Harold Ingrams got roughly 1,400 signatures to a three-year truce in the Hadhramaut in 1937, and Britain then built roads, schools and a Hadhrami Bedouin Legion behind it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Aden and Mukalla, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: None outside a handful of state councils appointed by rulers.

statusPeriods.label: Federation of South Arabia and the Protectorate of South Arabia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Sixteen western states plus Aden formed the Federation of South Arabia; the Hadhrami and Mahra states refused to join and were renamed the Protectorate of South Arabia. Britain kept defence, foreign affairs and the purse for both.
statusPeriods.franchise: The federal Council was made up of rulers' nominees. No one in the protectorates ever voted in a general election under British rule.

departures.how: Between June and September 1967 the National Liberation Front deposed every one of the twenty-odd rulers Britain had spent eighty years subsidising, mostly without a shot, and the sultanates were abolished before the British left.

led.name: Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi
led.role: NLF secretary-general; first president of South Yemen

led.name: Salim Rubai Ali
led.role: NLF commander in the countryside, later president of the PDRY, executed in 1978

led.name: Sultan Ghalib II bin Awadh al-Qu'aiti
led.role: last Qu'aiti Sultan of Mukalla, deposed by the NLF in September 1967 aged 19

cost.note: The sultanates fell with very little fighting: most rulers left for Saudi Arabia or Britain. Land was seized from the sada families of the Hadhramaut and thousands emigrated to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf in the years that followed.

departures.borders: The protectorate's inland boundaries were never surveyed at all; South Yemen inherited a frontier with Saudi Arabia that stayed undefined until the Treaty of Jeddah in 2000, and one with Oman that was disputed into the 1990s.

evidence.author: Glen Balfour-Paul
evidence.work: The End of Empire in the Middle East: Britain's Relinquishment of Power in her Last Three Arab Dependencies
evidence.supports: The collapse of the federation and the rulers Britain had backed.

violence.note: From 1919 Britain policed the protectorate by air: the RAF bombed villages and crops of rulers who refused to obey, a doctrine its own officers called 'air control' and defended as cheaper than soldiers.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Violet Line of 1914 divided Yemen for 76 years and its ghost still marks the split between north and south.
consequences.economicLegacy: Britain built roads and a legion but almost no schools: at independence the protectorate had a literacy rate in single figures and one hospital outside Mukalla.

peak.populationNote: There was never a census. The 1955 estimate of about 650,000 for both protectorates comes from British administrative guesswork and could be out by a third in either direction.
exports: remittances from Hadhrami migrants in Java and Singapore

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Aden Protectorate’s largest recorded population: 650,000 people, counted in 1955.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: R. J. Gavin
evidence.work: Aden Under British Rule, 1839-1967
evidence.supports: The protectorate treaty system from 1839 to 1967.

evidence.author: Spencer Mawby
evidence.work: British Policy in Aden and the Protectorates 1955-67: Last Outpost of a Middle East Empire
evidence.supports: The Federation, the advisory treaties and the collapse.

contested.note: Neither the start date nor the extent of the Aden Protectorate can be stated precisely. Britain counted between 20 and 90 separate treaty states depending on the year and the clerk, and much of the drawn area was never administered by anyone.

pedagogy.hook: Britain signed protection treaties with about ninety rulers in the hills behind Aden and then deposed exactly none of them. In 1967 a guerrilla movement removed the lot in four months.

misconception.belief: A protectorate is a colony under a politer name.
misconception.correction: A protectorate left the ruler on his throne and his subjects as his subjects, not British ones. Britain took only foreign relations, and often did not even administer the ground. In the Aden Protectorate that meant eighty years of stipends and air raids, and no schools, courts or tax system worth the name.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cheap indirect rule looked like a bargain and left nothing behind that could survive the day Britain went home. The sultanates fell in weeks because they had never been anything but a British payroll.

keyDates.what: First protection treaty, with the Mahra sultan
The Violet Line divides Yemen between Britain and the Ottomans
Ingrams' truce in the Hadhramaut; advisory treaties begin
The sultanates are abolished; South Yemen is proclaimed

territories.name: Perim
territories.formalName: Perim Island (Mayyun), a dependency of Aden

from.note: A rough marker for the island's Arabic name, which is far older than any British record of it.

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: Part of South Yemen from 1967 and of united Yemen since 1990. Fought over again in the war after 2015 because of what it commands.

geoCoverage.label: Lighthouse, coal store and garrison
geoCoverage.change: Britain came back to the same 13-square-kilometre rock 58 years later, this time to stay, because steam power had made the Bab al-Mandab strait the door to the Red Sea.

acquisitions.how: The East India Company landed troops from Bombay on the waterless island to block Bonaparte's army in Egypt from reaching India through the Red Sea; they found no fresh water and withdrew to Aden within four months.

counterparties.name: No settled population
counterparties.note: Perim had no permanent inhabitants: no fresh water. Fishermen from the Yemeni and Djibouti coasts used it seasonally, and the Sultan of Lahej claimed it.

evidence.author: R. J. Gavin
evidence.work: Aden Under British Rule, 1839-1967
evidence.supports: The 1799 occupation and the 1857 return.

acquisitions.how: A detachment from the Aden garrison landed and hoisted the flag, and Britain annexed the island to the Aden Settlement; a lighthouse followed in 1861 and a coaling station in the 1880s.

counterparties.name: The Sultan of Lahej and the Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Both claimed Perim and neither was consulted; Britain simply held the island and no one could dislodge it.

acquisitions.resistance: None on the island. France protested, having considered the same rock for its own coaling station on the route to Indochina.

contested.note: A well-worn story says British officers occupied Perim days or hours ahead of a French expedition and toasted the French captain over dinner. It is repeated in many books and rests on very thin contemporary evidence; treat it as a good anecdote, not a fact.

evidence.author: R. J. Gavin
evidence.work: Aden Under British Rule, 1839-1967
evidence.supports: The reoccupation of 1857 and its strategic reasoning.

statusPeriods.label: Four months against Napoleon
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Company garrison held the island under military orders from Bombay and left when its water ran out.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody lived there.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed to the Aden Settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Aden Resident administered the island for the East India Company; the population was the garrison, the lighthouse keepers and the coal heavers.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain abandoned Perim in 1799 and no British authority existed on the island for 58 years.

statusPeriods.label: A dependency of Aden, under India
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Government of India ran Perim through Aden. The Perim Coal Company bunkered ships from 1883 and for a while sold more coal than Aden itself.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Part of the Colony of Aden
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Perim passed with Aden to the Colonial Office. Its coal trade died as ships switched to oil, and by the 1950s the island was a lighthouse, a wireless station and a few hundred people.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Perim went out with Aden on 30 November 1967 and became part of the People's Republic of South Yemen, which promptly discovered it now controlled one side of the strait through which most of Europe's oil passed.

led.name: Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi
led.role: NLF secretary-general who took over Aden and its islands

cost.note: Nobody was killed on Perim. The island's people were evacuated to the mainland when the lighthouse and cable station closed.

departures.borders: Perim sits in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab and splits the strait into a 3-kilometre and a 25-kilometre channel; whoever holds it can close the Red Sea, which is exactly why Britain took it twice.

evidence.author: Glen Balfour-Paul
evidence.work: The End of Empire in the Middle East: Britain's Relinquishment of Power in her Last Three Arab Dependencies
evidence.supports: The 1967 withdrawal and Aden's dependencies.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Perim Coal Company employed several hundred Somali and Yemeni labourers from 1883 until oil-burning ships killed the trade in the 1930s; the island has been almost empty since.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's claim, never accepted by Yemen or the Ottomans, is why Perim is Yemeni and not Djiboutian or Eritrean today.

peak.populationNote: A guess from the coaling-station era; the 1931 Aden census gives about 1,500, almost all of them coal workers and their families.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Perim’s largest recorded population: 1,500 people, counted in 1931.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: R. J. Gavin
evidence.work: Aden Under British Rule, 1839-1967
evidence.supports: Perim's two occupations and its coaling trade.

pedagogy.hook: Britain occupied this waterless rock in 1799 to stop Napoleon, gave up after four months, and came back in 1857 the moment steamships made it the lock on the Red Sea.

misconception.belief: The empire grew steadily outwards from Britain, adding land year by year.
misconception.correction: It lurched. Perim was taken, abandoned for 58 years, then retaken when a new technology - the steam engine - changed what a barren island was worth. Empire followed engineering as much as ambition.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Perim explains what strategic points are for. The island had no people, no water and no trade of its own, and Britain held it for 110 years because of the two channels on either side of it.

keyDates.what: First occupation, to block Napoleon's route to India
Britain returns and annexes Perim to Aden
Lighthouse lit at the Bab al-Mandab
Handed over with Aden to South Yemen

territories.name: Kamaran
territories.formalName: Kamaran Island, administered from Aden

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: Taken by South Yemen in 1967, seized by North Yemen in 1972, and part of united Yemen since 1990.

acquisitions.how: An Indian Army and Royal Navy force took the island from its small Ottoman garrison during the First World War, mainly to keep control of the quarantine station every pilgrim ship to Mecca had to call at.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Istanbul lost the quarantine station that gave it authority over the sea route to the Hajj, and the customs revenue that came with it.

counterparties.name: The islanders of Kamaran
counterparties.lost: About 2,000 fishermen and salt workers passed from Ottoman to British administration without being asked, and stayed under it for 52 years.

acquisitions.resistance: None recorded on the island; the Ottoman garrison surrendered.

evidence.author: Eugene Rogan
evidence.work: The Fall of the Ottomans: The Great War in the Middle East
evidence.supports: British operations against Ottoman positions on the Red Sea coast in 1915.

statusPeriods.label: Held for 52 years without ever deciding what it was
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain never annexed Kamaran or declared a protectorate over it. The Government of India, and from 1949 the Governor of Aden, simply appointed an officer who ran the quarantine station, the courts and the police, while lawyers in London argued about what the island's status actually was.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Kamaran had a British administrator and no representative body of any kind.
statusPeriods.note: Up to 30,000 pilgrims a year were held at the Kamaran quarantine camp before being allowed on to Jeddah. Egypt, the Netherlands and British India jointly funded it; Britain ran it.

departures.how: Britain left with the rest of the Aden withdrawal and the People's Republic of South Yemen took the island, although it lies 600 kilometres up the Red Sea coast, off North Yemen.

led.name: Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi
led.role: NLF leader whose new state inherited Britain's Red Sea islands

cost.note: No one died in the handover. The quarantine station had already closed as pilgrims switched to aircraft.

departures.borders: Britain's 52-year occupation left Kamaran attached to the state 600 kilometres to its south rather than to the North Yemeni coast a few kilometres away, and North Yemen took it by force in 1972.

contested.note: Accounts differ on exactly when North Yemen took Kamaran from South Yemen: most say 1972, during the first war between the two Yemens. The 1967 British handover to the South is well attested; what happened next is thinly documented.

evidence.author: Glen Balfour-Paul
evidence.work: The End of Empire in the Middle East: Britain's Relinquishment of Power in her Last Three Arab Dependencies
evidence.supports: The scope of the 1967 withdrawal from Aden and its dependencies.

consequences.economicLegacy: The island lived on the quarantine camp and a salt works; both were gone by the 1960s, and Kamaran has been poor and marginal ever since.
consequences.borderLegacy: A British administrative decision left a Red Sea island attached to South Yemen, which is why it was fought over in 1972.

territories.formalName: The Mahra Sultanate of Qishn and Socotra, a protected state of the Eastern Aden Protectorate

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: A Yemeni governorate since 2013. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 2008 for plants found nowhere else.

geoCoverage.label: Protected, then protectorate
geoCoverage.change: Britain came back 41 years later not to occupy the island but to buy an undertaking that its sultan would never sell it to anyone else - a cheaper way of keeping the French and Ottomans off the sea road to India.

acquisitions.how: When the Mahra sultan refused to sell the island, the East India Company landed troops anyway to build a coaling station for the new Bombay-Suez steamer route; fever and dysentery killed enough of them that Britain evacuated within sixteen months and took Aden instead.

counterparties.name: The Soqotri people
counterparties.lost: A population of a few thousand herders and fishermen, speaking a South Arabian language unrelated to Arabic, found a garrison on their coast for over a year.

acquisitions.resistance: The islanders withdrew inland and would not trade with the garrison, which was one reason it starved and sickened.

counterparties.lost: He gave the islands away himself, to keep Britain friendly; his successors spent a century trying to get them back and their fishermen lost the guano the islands were worth.

territories.name: Kuwait
territories.formalName: The Sheikhdom of Kuwait, a British protected state

from.note: The Bani Utub settled the site early in the eighteenth century; no exact founding date is recorded.

modernSuccessors.name: Kuwait
modernSuccessors.note: Invaded and annexed by Iraq on 2 August 1990 and restored by a US-led coalition in February 1991 - the second time Britain sent troops to stop an Iraqi claim to Kuwait.

geoCoverage.label: The sheikhdom at the head of the Gulf

acquisitions.how: Sheikh Mubarak Al-Sabah, who had taken Kuwait by killing his two half-brothers in 1896 and feared Ottoman retribution, secretly bound himself and his heirs never to cede territory or receive a foreign agent without British consent, in return for protection and 15,000 rupees.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Istanbul claimed Kuwait as a district of the Basra vilayet and lost it: the 1899 agreement was kept secret precisely so the Sultan could not object, and Ottoman authority there never recovered.

counterparties.name: The German Empire and the Baghdad Railway company
counterparties.lost: Kuwait Bay was the intended Gulf terminus of the Berlin-to-Baghdad railway. The 1899 agreement killed that plan and with it Germany's route to the Indian Ocean.

counterparties.name: The Al-Sabah ruling family and the merchants of Kuwait
counterparties.lost: They kept full internal power and gained protection, and gave up the right to deal with any state but Britain - a bargain Mubarak sought rather than suffered.

instrument.name: Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 1899
instrument.note: Negotiated by Malcolm Meade, the Political Resident in the Persian Gulf, and kept secret from the Ottomans for years.

people.name: Mubarak Al-Sabah
people.role: Sheikh of Kuwait, called Mubarak the Great; sought British protection to secure a throne he had seized

people.name: Malcolm Meade
people.role: Political Resident in the Persian Gulf who negotiated the agreement

acquisitions.resistance: The opposition was Ottoman and German, not Kuwaiti; Mubarak wanted the deal. Kuwaiti merchants protested against his taxes in 1910, and again in 1938 when the Majlis movement demanded an elected assembly.

evidence.author: Jill Crystal
evidence.work: Oil and Politics in the Gulf: Rulers and Merchants in Kuwait and Qatar
evidence.supports: The 1899 agreement and the ruler-merchant bargain it rested on.

statusPeriods.label: British protected state under the Al-Sabah
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Sheikh governed Kuwait and Britain governed Kuwait's outside world. A Political Agent arrived in 1904; Britain ran foreign policy, defence and the oil concession, and never collected a tax or appointed a judge over Kuwaitis.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuwait Town, under the Political Resident in the Persian Gulf at Bushire
statusPeriods.franchise: None under British protection. An elected Legislative Council was set up by Kuwaiti reformers in 1938 and dissolved by the ruler within six months, with British backing.
statusPeriods.note: Oil was found at Burgan in February 1938 and exported from 1946. The Kuwait Oil Company was half BP, half Gulf Oil - Britain insisted on a British share of any concession as a condition of protection.

departures.how: Britain and Sheikh Abdullah III exchanged letters cancelling the 1899 agreement; six days later Iraq's Abd al-Karim Qasim claimed Kuwait as Iraqi territory, and Britain landed 6,000 troops in Operation Vantage before handing over to an Arab League force.

pedagogy.hook: Kuwait asked to be protected. In 1899 a ruler who had murdered his way to the throne signed himself into Britain's empire to keep the Ottomans and a German railway out.

misconception.belief: Britain forced its protection on unwilling rulers everywhere in the Gulf.
misconception.correction: In the northern Gulf the rulers often did the asking. territories.name: Bahrain
territories.formalName: The Sheikhdom of Bahrain, a British protected state

modernSuccessors.name: Bahrain
modernSuccessors.note: A kingdom since 2002. The US Fifth Fleet occupies the base Britain left, and the Royal Navy returned to Mina Salman in 2018.

geoCoverage.label: The archipelago and its pearl banks

acquisitions.how: After a Royal Navy and Bombay Marine expedition had burned the Qawasim fleet at Ras al-Khaimah, Bahrain's rulers signed the same General Maritime Treaty as the Trucial sheikhs, accepting British policing of the sea and a British definition of piracy.

counterparties.name: The Al Khalifa rulers of Bahrain
counterparties.lost: They lost the right to fight at sea, to raid, and eventually to conduct any foreign relations; in exchange the Royal Navy guaranteed them against Persia, the Ottomans and the Al Saud.

counterparties.name: The Baharna, Bahrain's indigenous Shia villagers and pearl divers
counterparties.lost: British protection froze in place an Al Khalifa order under which Baharna villagers paid a forced-labour levy and had no access to the ruler's courts; reform came only after 1923, and then by British fiat.

instrument.name: General Maritime Treaty of 1820
instrument.note: Signed by the Trucial sheikhs from 8 January 1820 and by Bahrain on 23 February 1820.

evidence.author: James Onley
evidence.work: The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj: Merchants, Rulers, and the British in the Nineteenth-Century Gulf
evidence.supports: The 1820 treaty system and Bahrain's place in it.

acquisitions.how: Sheikh Isa bin Ali bound himself not to deal with any government but Britain's, and confirmed it in a fuller exclusive agreement on 13 March 1892, turning a naval truce into a protectorate in everything but name.

counterparties.name: Sheikh Isa bin Ali Al Khalifa
counterparties.lost: He gave up all external relations, and in 1923 Britain deposed him for refusing administrative reform - proving how much the bargain had actually cost his family.

counterparties.name: Persia and the Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Both claimed Bahrain. The agreements shut both out; Iran maintained its claim until 1970.

instrument.name: Exclusive Agreements of 1880 and 1892

statusPeriods.label: Under the maritime truce
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain policed the sea and left the land alone. The Royal Navy suppressed raiding and the Al Khalifa fought their own wars ashore, twice losing and regaining the islands.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bushire, in Persia, where the Political Resident lived
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Perpetual Truce, then exclusive agreements
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1861 Perpetual Truce made Britain responsible for Bahrain's protection at sea; a Political Agent was posted to Manama in 1900, and British courts took jurisdiction over foreigners in Bahrain, which by the 1920s meant most of the merchant class.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Manama, under the Political Resident in the Persian Gulf
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: In May 1923 Britain deposed Sheikh Isa bin Ali and installed his son Hamad, after protests by Persian and Najdi merchants and Baharna villagers against the ruler's administration. It was the most direct British intervention in any Gulf state.

statusPeriods.label: Run by the Adviser: the Belgrave era and after
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Charles Belgrave arrived in 1926 as Adviser to the ruler and stayed 31 years, running the courts, the police, the budget and the oil revenues. In practice Bahrain was administered by one Englishman with no formal British authority at all.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the usual 2 for a protected state: from 1926 to 1957 a British Adviser actually ran Bahrain's internal administration, which no other Gulf protected state experienced for so long.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The National Union Committee of 1954-56 demanded an elected assembly and a labour law; Britain and the ruler banned it in November 1956 after the Suez protests and deported three of its leaders to Saint Helena.
statusPeriods.note: Oil was struck at Jebel Dukhan on 2 June 1932 - the first commercial oil field on the Arab side of the Gulf, six years before Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

departures.how: After Britain announced in 1968 that it was leaving the Gulf, Bahrain refused to join the federation Britain proposed and declared independence on its own, having first settled Iran's claim by a UN survey that found Bahrainis wanted neither Iran nor Britain.

contested.note: Oman is the hardest classification case in the Gulf. It appears on almost no list of British possessions, yet Britain fought two wars there, commanded its army, and replaced its ruler in 1970. Whether to colour it on a map of the empire is a real historiographical argument, not a technicality.

pedagogy.hook: Oman was never a British colony, never a protectorate and never on any Colonial Office list. In 1970 British officers helped remove its sultan and put his son on the throne.

misconception.belief: You can tell what Britain ruled by colouring in the pink bits.
misconception.correction: Informal empire does not colour in. Oman was legally sovereign for the whole period and yet could not sell land, grant an oil concession, or keep a ruler Britain had decided against. Ask what a government could actually do, not what the map says.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Oman is the clearest case of informal empire in the Middle East, and it lasted longest: the last British officers left Omani command posts in the 1980s, long after every formal possession in the region had gone.

territories.formalName: The Emirate of Nejd and Hasa (later the Sultanate of Nejd), a British protected state

modernSuccessors.name: Saudi Arabia
modernSuccessors.note: Ibn Saud's Nejd absorbed the Hejaz in 1925 and the two were renamed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. Standard Oil of California, not a British company, got the oil concession in 1933.

counterparties.lost: He gave up independent foreign relations and the right to attack Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar or the Trucial coast, and gained recognition, money and weapons that let him conquer the rest of Arabia.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: It lost its remaining claim to eastern Arabia and the Gulf coast, which it had reoccupied in 1871 and lost again in 1913.

counterparties.name: The Rashidi Emirate of Hail
counterparties.lost: Britain's rival in central Arabia, backed by the Ottomans; with British money behind Ibn Saud it was destroyed in 1921.

territories.name: Iraq
territories.formalName: Occupied Mesopotamia, then the British Mandate for Mesopotamia and the Kingdom of Iraq

namesOverTime.name: The vilayets of Basra, Baghdad and Mosul

from.note: The three provinces were Ottoman from the sixteenth century; the exact administrative boundaries changed repeatedly.

namesOverTime.name: Mesopotamia
namesOverTime.note: The name in every British document until the state was named; the mandate itself was 'for Mesopotamia'.

namesOverTime.name: Al-Iraq
namesOverTime.note: An old Arabic name for the alluvial lowlands, adopted for the new kingdom.

modernSuccessors.name: Iraq
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since the revolution of 14 July 1958. Britain invaded again in 1941 and, with the United States, in 2003.

geoCoverage.label: Conquered province by province
geoCoverage.change: Britain landed at Fao on 6 November 1914 and took Basra, Baghdad in March 1917 and Mosul only after the armistice; for four years the drawn shape is a front line, not a border.

geoCoverage.label: Occupied Mesopotamia, then the mandate
geoCoverage.change: With Mosul occupied after the armistice, Britain held all three Ottoman provinces and joined them into a single state that had never existed before.

geoCoverage.label: Independent, with British air bases
geoCoverage.change: Iraq became sovereign, and Britain kept the right to move troops through it and to hold the air bases at Habbaniya and Shaibah under the treaty of 1930.

geoCoverage.label: Reoccupied
geoCoverage.change: Britain invaded the country it had made independent, beat Rashid Ali's army in a month, and kept troops in Iraq for six more years.

geoCoverage.label: Bases and a British-aligned monarchy
geoCoverage.change: The combat troops left and the air bases stayed, until the revolution of 14 July 1958 swept away the monarchy and the bases with it.

acquisitions.how: Indian Expeditionary Force D, sent from Bombay to protect the Anglo-Persian oil refinery at Abadan, landed at Fao and took Basra on 22 November 1914; four years of fighting up the Tigris and Euphrates followed.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: It lost the three provinces of Basra, Baghdad and Mosul, which it had ruled for nearly four centuries, and the oil of Kirkuk it had never exploited.

counterparties.name: The people of Mesopotamia
counterparties.lost: Between 1914 and 1918 the campaign killed tens of thousands of civilians through fighting, requisitioning and famine, and the Bani Huchaim and the other confederations of the mid-Euphrates lost the autonomy the Ottomans had left them.

people.name: Charles Townshend

people.role: commanded the force that took Baghdad in March 1917 and died of cholera there in November

people.name: Khalil Pasha
people.role: Ottoman commander who took the surrender at Kut

evidence.work: A History of Iraq

acquisitions.how: At San Remo the Allied powers assigned Mesopotamia to Britain as a League of Nations Class A mandate; the news reached Baghdad in May and the country rose in revolt in June.

counterparties.name: The people of Iraq
counterparties.lost: They had been promised self-determination in the Anglo-French Declaration of 7 November 1918 and were given a mandate instead, administered by British officials with an Indian civil-service model.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Under Sykes-Picot Mosul had been in the French zone; Clemenceau handed it to Lloyd George in December 1918 in exchange for a share of its oil.
counterparties.note: The deal was confirmed in the San Remo oil agreement of 24 April 1920: France got 25% of the Turkish Petroleum Company.

instrument.name: San Remo resolution assigning the Mandate for Mesopotamia
instrument.note: The mandate text was approved by the League Council only on 24 July 1922, and Britain governed Iraq instead through the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 10 October 1922.

people.name: Arnold Wilson
people.role: acting Civil Commissioner who ran Mesopotamia on Indian lines and dismissed Iraqi demands for self-rule

people.name: Gertrude Bell
people.role: Oriental Secretary in Baghdad; drew much of Iraq's shape and chose its king

people.name: Percy Cox
people.role: High Commissioner from October 1920; installed Faisal and negotiated the 1922 treaty

contested.note: There is no single date on which Iraq became British. The occupation began in 1914; San Remo assigned the mandate in April 1920; the League approved the mandate text in July 1922; and Britain in fact governed through the treaty of October 1922, never formally applying the mandate instrument. Textbooks pick different dates and rarely explain why.

evidence.work: Britain in Iraq: Contriving King and Country
evidence.supports: The mandate, the 1922 treaty and how Britain actually governed Iraq.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation run on Indian lines
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The army governed. Political officers, mostly seconded from the Indian Political Service, collected revenue and settled disputes through shaikhs under the regulation Britain titled the Tribal Criminal and Civil Disputes Regulation, copied from the Punjab frontier.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Baghdad, under the Government of India until 1920, then the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: None. A referendum of sorts was held in 1918-19 by asking selected notables what government they wanted; the answers Britain did not like were not recorded.

statusPeriods.label: Kingdom of Iraq under British mandate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Faisal I reigned; a British High Commissioner decided. Every Iraqi ministry had a British adviser whose advice was binding, the budget needed British approval, and the RAF held the country together from the air under Trenchard's air-control scheme.
statusPeriods.franchise: An indirectly elected Chamber of Deputies from 1925, chosen through electoral colleges dominated by landowners and sheikhs. The first assembly ratified the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty by a narrow vote taken at four in the morning.
statusPeriods.note: Faisal had been made king of Syria and thrown out by France in July 1920; Britain then installed him in Baghdad after a plebiscite in which he was recorded as receiving 96% of the vote.

statusPeriods.label: Independent, with British bases and a British ambassador
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Iraq joined the League of Nations as a sovereign state. The 1930 treaty gave Britain two air bases, the right to move troops across the country in war, and a British military mission; the ambassador's opinion still decided cabinets.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above 0 for an informal sphere: this was formal independence with a treaty that gave Britain permanent bases and transit rights, which is more than influence and less than rule.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Baghdad, with a British Embassy and RAF Habbaniya
statusPeriods.franchise: Indirect two-stage elections dominated by landholders; governments were made and unmade by the palace and the army, not the polls.

statusPeriods.label: Invaded again, 1941
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Rashid Ali al-Gaylani's nationalist government besieged RAF Habbaniya in April 1941; Britain flew in reinforcements, defeated the Iraqi army in a month, restored the regent, and kept troops in the country until 1947.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Baghdad, under British military control with an Iraqi government in office
statusPeriods.franchise: Unchanged on paper. Martial law was in force and hundreds of nationalists were interned.
statusPeriods.note: In the two days after the Iraqi defeat, 1-2 June 1941, a mob attacked Baghdad's Jewish quarter in the pogrom known as the Farhud while British troops halted outside the city. At least 180 Jews were killed; some estimates run much higher.

statusPeriods.label: Bases, oil and the Baghdad Pact
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British troops left but the RAF kept Habbaniya and Shaibah, the Iraq Petroleum Company kept the oil, and the government of Nuri al-Said kept Iraq inside Britain's defence system - the Portsmouth Treaty of 1948 was torn up after riots, but the Baghdad Pact of 1955 did the same job.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above 0 because Britain retained air bases and treaty rights until the 1958 revolution: influence backed by an airfield.
statusPeriods.franchise: Elections were routinely managed. The Wathba uprising of January 1948 against the Portsmouth Treaty killed several hundred people in Baghdad and forced the treaty's abandonment.

departures.how: Iraq entered the League of Nations as the first mandate to become independent, on terms set by the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 30 June 1930: Britain kept two air bases, transit rights and a military mission for 25 years.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Iraq Petroleum Company, controlled from London by a consortium in which British interests held the largest share, paid Iraq a fixed royalty per ton and kept the profit; Iraq nationalised it in 1972.

commonwealth.note: As a mandate, not a colony, Iraq never joined the Commonwealth.

pedagogy.hook: Iraq was the first country in history to be policed from the air. From 1922 the RAF bombed villages that would not pay tax, because aircraft were cheaper than soldiers.

modernSuccessors.note: The West Bank was annexed by Jordan in 1950 and occupied by Israel in 1967; Gaza was under Egyptian military administration from 1948 and occupied by Israel in 1967. Neither has been a sovereign state in practice.

geoCoverage.label: The advance from Beersheba to Jerusalem and north

counterparties.lost: It lost the sanjaks of Jerusalem, Nablus and Acre after four centuries, along with the Hejaz Railway and its authority over the holy places.

counterparties.name: The Arab population of Palestine
counterparties.lost: About 90% of the country's roughly 700,000 people in 1917, they lost the promise of self-determination made to Sharif Hussein, and gained a government committed by the Balfour Declaration to building a national home for another people in their country.

counterparties.name: The Jewish population of Palestine
counterparties.lost: About 60,000 people in 1917, many of them expelled or impoverished under Ottoman wartime rule; the Balfour Declaration made Britain the sponsor of Zionist settlement, and Britain then restricted that immigration in 1939 as the Nazi persecution reached its height.

statusPeriods.franchise: An Advisory Council of officials and nominees. Palestinian Arabs refused seats on any body that implied acceptance of the mandate, and so had no representative institution at all for 28 years.
statusPeriods.note: The White Paper of June 1922 restricted immigration to the country's 'economic absorptive capacity' - the formula that governed the argument for the next 17 years.

statusPeriods.label: The Mandate for Palestine
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A High Commissioner governed by ordinance with no elected legislature at all, reporting to the Colonial Office and answering annually to the League's Permanent Mandates Commission. statusPeriods.franchise: There was never a general election in mandatory Palestine. Municipal elections were held on a restricted property franchise.
statusPeriods.note: The Jewish population rose from about 84,000 in 1922 to 608,000 in 1946 - from 11% to 31% of the population - through immigration Britain first encouraged and then, from the White Paper of May 1939, restricted to 75,000 over five years as European Jews were being murdered.

departures.how: Unable to hold Palestine against a Jewish insurgency and an Arab revolt, and unwilling to impose the UN partition plan of 29 November 1947, Britain handed the problem to the United Nations, set a date, and left at midnight on 14 May 1948 without transferring authority to anyone.

Around 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians left or were expelled from their homes, in the events Palestinians call the Nakba; UN estimates at the time were about 720,000. Benny Morris's revised study (2004) documents expulsions in dozens of villages alongside flight from fear and collapse. departures.borders: Britain left no border at all. contested.note: Palestine is the most contested entry in this atlas. The disagreement is not only about numbers but about the frame: whether the mandate was a well-meant impossibility, a colonial project with a Zionist partner, or a betrayal of promises made to the Arabs in 1915. The evidence for the events is largely agreed; the meaning is not.

pedagogy.hook: Britain promised the same land twice: to Sharif Hussein in 1915 in exchange for an Arab revolt, and to the Zionist movement in 1917 in a single sentence signed by the Foreign Secretary.

misconception.belief: Britain tried to be neutral in Palestine and the two sides simply could not agree.
misconception.correction: Britain was not a referee. It wrote the Balfour Declaration into the mandate, ran the immigration quota that decided the country's demography, and then reversed itself in 1939 and shut the gates as European Jews were being murdered. Both communities ended up fighting Britain as well as each other, which is what happens when the umpire is also a player.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Every unresolved question in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - borders, refugees, Jerusalem, who has the right to decide - was framed between 1917 and 1948 by British decisions, and Britain left in 1948 without settling any of them.

namesOverTime.name: Sharq al-Urdunn (Transjordan)

modernSuccessors.name: Jordan
modernSuccessors.note: The only Arab mandate that emerged with its dynasty, borders and institutions intact, and the only one still ruled by the family Britain installed.

statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Eight months of nobody in charge

statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Almost no British authority existed: officials themselves described Transjordan in this period as ungoverned, and one wrote that Britain's policy was to have none.
statusPeriods.franchise: Local councils of notables, self-appointed, in Salt, Irbid, Karak and Amman - the only period of self-government Transjordan had before 1946.

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Amman, under the High Commissioner in Jerusalem
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Treaty government under British advice

statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the mandate default of 4: from 1928 Transjordan had its own constitution, a partly elected council and an Arab government, with Britain holding foreign affairs, finance and the army.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council partly elected from 1929 on a limited male franchise with seats reserved by community; the Emir could dissolve it and did.

departures.how: The Treaty of London of 22 March 1946 ended the mandate and Abdullah was proclaimed King on 25 May; Britain kept two air bases, a military mission and the right to station troops, and went on paying for the Arab Legion until 1957.

acquisitions.how: Fifteen days after the Armistice of Mudros an Allied fleet of 55 ships led by the Royal Navy anchored off Constantinople and landed troops; a British general took charge of the police and the ports of the capital of a 600-year-old empire.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Its capital, its army, its navy, its remaining Arab provinces and finally its existence: the sultanate was abolished by the Ankara assembly on 1 November 1922 and Mehmed VI left on a British warship.

counterparties.name: The people of Constantinople
counterparties.lost: About a million people came under foreign military police, censorship and courts martial, and the city filled with roughly 200,000 refugees, including White Russians fleeing the civil war.

instrument.name: Armistice of Mudros
instrument.note: Article 7 let the Allies occupy any point they judged threatening; Britain used it to take the Straits, the Baku oilfields and Mosul.

people.name: Somerset Gough-Calthorpe
people.role: British admiral who signed the Mudros armistice and commanded the occupation

people.name: Mehmed VI
people.role: last Ottoman sultan; left Constantinople aboard HMS Malaya on 17 November 1922

people.name: Mustafa Kemal
people.role: Ottoman general who left the occupied capital in May 1919 and organised the national resistance in Anatolia

acquisitions.resistance: The Turkish national movement, formed in Anatolia from 1919, refused the armistice terms; when Britain formally occupied the city on 16 March 1920 and arrested nationalist deputies, the survivors reconvened in Ankara as the Grand National Assembly on 23 April 1920.

evidence.author: Nur Bilge Criss
evidence.work: Istanbul under Allied Occupation, 1918-1923
evidence.supports: The course and administration of the occupation.

statusPeriods.label: De facto occupation, government still sitting
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Allied high commissioners supervised while the Sultan's government continued to sit and issue decrees. Britain, France and Italy each policed a sector of the city and jointly controlled the ports, the railway and the press.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the 5 an occupation usually means: the Ottoman government continued to govern, and Britain shared control with France and Italy rather than holding it alone.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The British High Commission at Constantinople
statusPeriods.franchise: The Ottoman Chamber of Deputies was elected in late 1919 and adopted the National Pact in January 1920, which is why the Allies dissolved it.

statusPeriods.label: Formal occupation and martial law
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British troops seized the ministries, the telegraph and the arsenal on 16 March 1920, arrested about 150 nationalists and deported many to Malta. From then the Allies governed the capital directly and the Sultan's government did what it was told.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Still below 5 because it remained a three-power occupation with an Ottoman government nominally in office, though after March 1920 the Allies gave the orders.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Allied High Commissions, Britain in the lead
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The real Turkish parliament was now in Ankara, outside Allied reach.

departures.how: The Turkish national army destroyed the Greek forces in Anatolia in September 1922 and then faced British troops at Chanak; Britain's cabinet wanted to fight, its dominions and its commander on the spot refused, and the Allies negotiated instead, leaving Istanbul on 6 October 1923.

led.name: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk
led.role: led the Turkish national movement and the war that forced the Allies out; first president of the Republic

led.name: Ismet Inonu
led.role: commanded at Inonu and negotiated the Treaty of Lausanne for Turkey

led.name: Charles Harington
led.role: British commander at Chanak who refused to deliver the ultimatum his cabinet had ordered

led.name: David Lloyd George
led.role: prime minister whose Turkish policy collapsed at Chanak and brought down his government on 19 October 1922

departures.movement: The Turkish national movement and the Grand National Assembly at Ankara

cost.note: The Greco-Turkish war of 1919-22, fought partly at Allied instigation, killed hundreds of thousands of Greek and Turkish soldiers and civilians; the burning of Smyrna in September 1922 alone killed an estimated 10,000 to 100,000. The Lausanne convention of 30 January 1923 then compelled the exchange of about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians and 400,000 Muslims. All these figures are disputed.

departures.borders: Lausanne fixed Turkey's borders almost as they are today, cancelling the partition of Anatolia agreed at Sevres in 1920. It also left the promise of a Kurdish state, made at Sevres, out of the final treaty entirely.

instrument.name: Treaty of Lausanne
instrument.note: It replaced the Treaty of Sevres of 10 August 1920, which the Turkish national movement had refused to accept and which was never ratified.

evidence.author: A. L. Macfie
evidence.work: The End of the Ottoman Empire, 1908-1923
evidence.supports: The occupation, Sevres, Chanak and Lausanne.

populationTransfer.note: The Treaty of Lausanne, which Britain signed, made the compulsory exchange of about 1.6 million people between Greece and Turkey legal - the first such exchange written into an international treaty, and the model cited for later partitions.

consequences.borderLegacy: Sevres promised the Kurds autonomy and possible independence; Lausanne, three years later, did not mention them. Kurdish nationalists have cited the difference ever since.

peak.populationNote: An estimate for occupied Constantinople and the Straits zones; the city's own population was swollen by refugees and is variously given between 800,000 and 1.2 million.

evidence.author: Nur Bilge Criss
evidence.work: Istanbul under Allied Occupation, 1918-1923
evidence.supports: The occupation regime and Turkish resistance to it.

evidence.author: A. L. Macfie
evidence.work: The End of the Ottoman Empire, 1908-1923
evidence.supports: Mudros, Sevres, Chanak and Lausanne.

pedagogy.hook: For nearly five years British troops policed Istanbul, and the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire left his own capital for the last time on board a British battleship.

misconception.belief: The British Empire only ever grew until 1945 and then shrank.
misconception.correction: It reached its greatest extent about 1920-22 and immediately started losing. Turkey took back Istanbul and Anatolia by force in 1922-23, Ireland left in 1922, Egypt was declared independent in 1922 and Afghanistan in 1919. The high point and the first defeats were the same three years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Chanak in September 1922 is the moment the empire discovered it could not fight another war: the dominions refused, the cabinet split, and Lloyd George's government fell. It is the first clear failure of the imperial system as a war-making machine.
