Formal occupation; nationalist deputies arrested and deported to Malta
The Chanak crisis: the dominions refuse to fight
The Treaty of Lausanne replaces Sevres
The last Allied troops leave Istanbul

territories.name: Persia and Iran
territories.formalName: Persia (Iran) under British informal empire

modernSuccessors.name: Iran
modernSuccessors.note: Persia asked to be called Iran internationally in 1935. Never colonised, and never fully independent of outside oil interests until 1979.

geoCoverage.label: Never a colony: factories, banks, oil and gunboats
geoCoverage.change: Drawn hatched throughout. Britain held no Persian territory except during brief wartime occupations; what it held was the customs of the Gulf ports, the country's only bank of issue, its oil, and after 1907 an agreed sphere in the south.

geoCoverage.label: Anglo-Soviet occupation
geoCoverage.change: British and Indian troops invaded from the south and Soviet forces from the north, deposed the Shah and used Iran as a supply corridor to the USSR - the only time Britain occupied Persian territory in force.

geoCoverage.label: Oil, and then the loss of it
geoCoverage.change: The troops left and the oil argument began: Iran nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951 and Britain, unable to reverse it alone, joined the United States in overthrowing the government that had done it.

acquisitions.how: Karim Khan Zand granted the East India Company a trading factory at Bushire with exemption from customs and the right to fortify it, and Bushire became the base from which Britain would run the Gulf for the next 183 years.

counterparties.name: Persia under the Zand dynasty
counterparties.lost: It gave up customs revenue and a measure of jurisdiction at its main southern port, in exchange for British help against the Dutch and a share of trade.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company
counterparties.lost: It was pushed out of the Persian Gulf trade within a decade.

evidence.author: J. B. Kelly
evidence.work: Britain and the Persian Gulf, 1795-1880
evidence.supports: The Bushire residency and Britain's position in southern Persia.

acquisitions.how: Britain and Russia divided Persia between themselves into a Russian sphere in the north, a British sphere in the south-east and a neutral zone in between, without consulting the Persian government, whose parliament had been elected only the year before.

counterparties.name: The Persian constitutional government
counterparties.lost: A country that had just won a constitution and a parliament in the revolution of 1905-06 found itself carved into spheres by two foreign powers; the Majlis protested and was ignored, and in 1911 Russian troops helped close it.

counterparties.name: Germany
counterparties.lost: The convention closed Persia to German influence and completed the Triple Entente encirclement Berlin had feared.

instrument.name: Anglo-Russian Convention

people.name: Edward Grey
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who negotiated the division of Persia

people.name: William Knox D'Arcy
people.role: speculator whose 1901 concession covered three quarters of Persia and produced the first Middle Eastern oil in 1908

people.name: Morgan Shuster
people.role: American treasurer-general hired by the Majlis in 1911 and forced out by a Russian ultimatum Britain supported

acquisitions.resistance: The Majlis rejected the convention; Persian constitutionalists fought both foreign spheres and their own shah, and were crushed when Russia bombarded the Majlis in 1908 and again in 1911.

evidence.author: Nikki R. Keddie
evidence.work: Modern Iran: Roots and Results of Revolution
evidence.supports: The 1907 convention, the constitutional revolution and Britain's role.

acquisitions.how: British and Indian forces invaded neutral Iran from Iraq and the Gulf while the Red Army came in from the north; within three weeks Reza Shah was forced to abdicate and was deported to Mauritius and then South Africa, where he died.

counterparties.name: Iran under Reza Shah
counterparties.lost: A neutral state was invaded, its ruler deposed and exiled, its railway taken over as a supply line to the Soviet Union, and its grain requisitioned; famine and typhus followed in 1942-43.

counterparties.name: Germany
counterparties.lost: It lost access to Iranian oil and the German technicians whose presence was Britain's stated pretext for the invasion.

instrument.name: Tripartite Treaty of Alliance between the United Kingdom, the USSR and Iran
instrument.note: It promised withdrawal within six months of the end of the war. Britain met the deadline; the USSR did not, and the resulting crisis in 1946 was the first case brought to the UN Security Council.

people.name: Reza Shah Pahlavi
people.role: deposed by Britain and the USSR in September 1941 and exiled; died in Johannesburg in 1944

people.name: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
people.role: installed by the Allies aged 21 and kept on the throne by the 1953 coup

cost.note: The invasion itself killed several hundred Iranian soldiers and about 22 British and 40 Soviet troops. Far worse followed: requisitioning and disruption of the harvest contributed to famine and typhus in 1942-43, with deaths estimated in the tens of thousands and no reliable count.

acquisitions.resistance: The Iranian army collapsed in three days. The political resistance came later, in the nationalist movement that grew out of the humiliation and produced Mossadegh.

evidence.author: Ashley Jackson
evidence.work: The British Empire and the Second World War
evidence.supports: The 1941 invasion and Iran as a wartime supply corridor.

statusPeriods.label: Factories, gunboats and telegraph lines
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain kept a residency at Bushire, ran the Indo-European Telegraph across Persia from 1865, made the Imperial Bank of Persia the country's bank of issue in 1889, and fought a short war in 1856-57 to force Persia out of Herat.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Persia governed itself; British interests were handled from Tehran, Bushire and Calcutta
statusPeriods.franchise: None until the constitutional revolution of 1906 created a Majlis on a limited, class-based franchise.

statusPeriods.label: A sphere of influence, and the oil
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Persia stayed sovereign and Britain controlled what mattered to it: the southern sphere agreed with Russia, the South Persia Rifles it raised in 1916, and from 1914 a majority stake, bought by the British government on Churchill's urging, in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above 0 because after 1907 Britain had an agreed sphere in southern Persia, raised its own military force there, and owned the country's largest industry outright.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Tehran, with a British legation and, in the south, British-officered levies
statusPeriods.franchise: The Majlis met and was repeatedly dissolved. The Anglo-Persian Agreement of 1919, which would have given Britain control of Persia's army and treasury, was rejected by the Majlis and never ratified - a rare and important British defeat.

statusPeriods.label: Anglo-Soviet occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain held the south and the oilfields, the Soviet Union the north, and Tehran was jointly garrisoned from 1943. An Iranian government continued in office and the Allies ran the railways, the ports and the grain supply.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below 5: this was a shared occupation with a functioning Iranian government in place, not direct rule.
statusPeriods.franchise: The Majlis continued to sit, and elections in 1943 and 1944 were freer than any since 1911 - one unintended result of the occupation.

statusPeriods.label: The oil crisis and the coup
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British troops left on time. The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company remained the largest enterprise in Iran, paying Britain more in tax than it paid Iran in royalties, until the Majlis nationalised it in March 1951 and Britain, with the United States, organised the overthrow of Mohammad Mossadegh.
statusPeriods.franchise: Mossadegh was elected prime minister by the Majlis in April 1951. After the coup of 19 August 1953 the Shah ruled with a secret police built with British and American help.

departures.how: Britain's paramountcy in Iran ended not with independence but with a handover: after the 1953 coup a new oil consortium gave American companies 40% and the renamed British Petroleum 40%, and Washington replaced London as the outside power that mattered in Tehran.

led.name: Mohammad Mossadegh
led.role: prime minister who nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951; overthrown in August 1953 and held under house arrest until his death

led.name: Kermit Roosevelt Jr
led.role: CIA officer who ran the 1953 coup, working with the British Secret Intelligence Service

led.name: Christopher Woodhouse
led.role: SIS officer who took the British coup plan to Washington after Britain was expelled from Iran

led.name: Fazlollah Zahedi
led.role: general installed as prime minister after the coup

departures.movement: The National Front and the oil nationalisation movement

cost.note: Around 200 to 300 people were killed in the street fighting of 19 August 1953 in Tehran, by most accounts. Britain's role was denied for sixty years; the CIA acknowledged its own part in 2013.

departures.borders: Iran's borders did not change. What changed was who controlled its oil: the 1954 consortium ended the British monopoly that had existed since D'Arcy's concession of 1901.

instrument.name: Consortium Agreement between Iran and an international group of oil companies
instrument.note: Ratified by the Majlis in October 1954. British Petroleum took 40%, five American majors 40%, Shell 14% and CFP of France 6%.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how far the 1953 coup was British and how far American, and about how close Mossadegh was to falling anyway. Ervand Abrahamian argues the initiative and the motive were largely British and about oil; other accounts stress American Cold War fears of communism.

evidence.author: Ervand Abrahamian
evidence.work: The Coup: 1953, the CIA, and the Roots of Modern U.S.-Iranian Relations
evidence.supports: The British origins of the coup and the oil dispute behind it.

consequences.economicLegacy: For forty years the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company took the great majority of the profits from Iran's oil; in 1950 it paid the British Treasury more in tax than it paid Iran in royalties. Abadan was the largest refinery in the world and Iranian workers there lived in segregated housing without piped water.
consequences.borderLegacy: The 1907 spheres left no border, but they taught a generation of Iranian nationalists that constitutional government could be undone by outside powers - an argument the 1953 coup then proved.

peak.populationNote: Iran's first census was in 1956 and gave 18.9 million; the 1941 figure is an estimate.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1941 census of Persia and Iran
populationWarrant.supports: Persia and Iran’s largest recorded population: 14,500,000 people, counted in 1941.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Nikki R. Keddie
evidence.work: Modern Iran: Roots and Results of Revolution
evidence.supports: Iranian politics under foreign pressure from 1900.

evidence.author: Ervand Abrahamian
evidence.work: The Coup: 1953, the CIA, and the Roots of Modern U.S.-Iranian Relations
evidence.supports: The oil dispute and the 1953 coup.

evidence.author: J. B. Kelly
evidence.work: Britain and the Persian Gulf, 1795-1880
evidence.supports: The nineteenth-century British position in the Gulf and southern Persia.

contested.note: Iran was never a British possession and appears on no map of the empire, yet Britain divided it into spheres in 1907, invaded and deposed its ruler in 1941, and helped overthrow its elected prime minister in 1953. Whether informal empire belongs in an atlas of empire is a real argument; this atlas includes it, hatched, and says why.

pedagogy.hook: Iran was never British, and yet in 1941 Britain deposed its ruler and in 1953 helped overthrow its elected prime minister for nationalising an oil company Britain owned.

misconception.belief: If a country was never coloured pink, the empire did not affect it.
misconception.correction: Informal empire could be as decisive as formal rule and left no mark on the map. In Iran, Britain owned the oil, ran the bank of issue, agreed a sphere of influence with Russia in 1907, invaded in 1941 and organised a coup in 1953. None of that would show on a map of British territory.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Iran is the best example of empire without colonies, and the 1953 coup is the clearest case of Britain's imperial reflexes outliving its power - it had to ask the Americans to do the job, and lost the oil monopoly anyway.

keyDates.what: Britain and Russia divide Persia into spheres
Oil found at Masjed Soleiman - the first in the Middle East
Anglo-Soviet invasion; Reza Shah deposed and exiled
Iran nationalises the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company
Mossadegh overthrown in a British and American coup

territories.name: Mauritius
territories.formalName: The Colony of Mauritius and its Dependencies

from.note: Portuguese navigators charted the uninhabited island early in the sixteenth century; the exact year and ship are disputed.

namesOverTime.name: Mauritius
namesOverTime.note: Named by the Dutch for Maurice of Nassau. They abandoned the island in 1710, having hunted the dodo to extinction and cut out the ebony.

namesOverTime.name: Mauritius / Maurice / Moris
namesOverTime.note: Britain restored the Dutch name; the island's languages did not change with its flag, and French and Creole are still spoken by almost everyone.

modernSuccessors.name: Mauritius
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 12 March 1992. Mauritius has claimed the Chagos Archipelago since 1968 and won an ICJ advisory opinion on it in 2019.

geoCoverage.label: Mauritius with Rodrigues and the Chagos dependencies
geoCoverage.change: The fall of Isle de France brought Britain the main island and everything the French had governed from it, including the Chagos Archipelago 2,200 kilometres to the north-east.

geoCoverage.label: Mauritius without the Chagos
geoCoverage.change: Three years before independence Britain detached the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius for £3 million and a fishing and mineral rights promise, to build an American base on Diego Garcia.

acquisitions.how: A force from Bombay under Lieutenant-Colonel Henry Keating landed on lightly held Rodrigues and turned it into the supply base for the invasion of Isle de France the following year.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: It lost the outer island that guarded the approach to Isle de France, and with it any hope of holding the Mascarenes.

counterparties.name: The settlers and enslaved people of Rodrigues
counterparties.lost: A population of about 100, most of them enslaved Africans and Malagasy, changed owners along with the island.

evidence.author: Auguste Toussaint
evidence.work: History of Mauritius
evidence.supports: The 1809-10 campaign in the Mascarenes.

acquisitions.how: About 10,000 British and Indian troops landed at Cap Malheureux on 29 November 1810 and General Charles Decaen capitulated four days later, ending twenty years in which French privateers based here had taken well over a hundred British merchant ships.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: It lost the Isle de France, its main naval base in the Indian Ocean, the corsair fleet that had preyed on British India trade, and Rodrigues, Seychelles and the Chagos with it.

counterparties.name: The enslaved population of the island
counterparties.lost: About 60,000 enslaved Africans, Malagasy and Indians were transferred with the colony. The capitulation guaranteed the French settlers their laws, religion and property - and their property was people. Slavery therefore lasted another 25 years.

counterparties.name: The French settler population
counterparties.lost: They lost their flag and kept everything else: the terms let them keep French civil law, the Catholic church, the French language and their estates, which is why Mauritius is a francophone country with a British constitution.

instrument.name: Capitulation of Isle de France

people.name: Charles Decaen
people.role: French governor-general who capitulated on terms

people.name: John Abercromby
people.role: commanded the British invasion force

people.name: Robert Townsend Farquhar
people.role: first British governor; suppressed the slave trade on paper and tolerated it in practice

cost.note: The 1810 landing cost about 170 British casualties. Four months earlier the British had lost the naval battle of Grand Port, the only French naval victory inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe, with four frigates lost and around 300 casualties.

warrant.author: The British and French naval commanders, in their own returns
warrant.work: British and French returns of the Mauritius campaign of 1810
warrant.supports: The 1810 landing cost about 170 British casualties. Four months earlier the British had lost the naval battle of Grand Port, the only French naval victory inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe, with four frigates lost and around 300 casualties.
warrant.check: ADM and WO series at The National Archives, Kew; the French figures for Grand Port are the ones inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe.
warrant.note: Both navies counted, and both counts survive, which is rare enough in this atlas to be worth saying.

acquisitions.resistance: The French garrison of some 1,300 regulars and militia fought two short actions and surrendered; the enslaved majority were not consulted and gained nothing.

evidence.author: Vijaya Teelock
evidence.work: Mauritian History: From Its Beginnings to Modern Times
evidence.supports: The conquest, the capitulation terms and their consequences for slavery.

acquisitions.how: At the Treaty of Paris France ceded Mauritius, Rodrigues and the Seychelles to Britain permanently, and got Reunion back - Britain kept the harbour and the sugar island it wanted and returned the one it did not.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: It gave up the Mascarene base it had held for a century, keeping only Reunion, which had no natural harbour.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris, 1814

evidence.author: Auguste Toussaint
evidence.work: History of Mauritius
evidence.supports: The 1814 settlement and what Britain kept.

statusPeriods.label: Conquest and military government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British governor ruled under the terms of the capitulation, keeping French law, French officials and the slave economy intact while the war continued.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Louis, under the Government of India
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Roughly four fifths of the population were enslaved.

statusPeriods.label: Crown Colony with a planter council
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed from London ruled with a council of officials and nominated planters. Sugar was everything: the estates set the wages, the labour laws and the police, and the colonial state enforced the indenture contracts that supplied them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Louis, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: A property and income franchise from 1885 gave the vote to about 2% of adults - roughly 4,000 men, almost all of them Franco-Mauritian or Creole property owners. Indo-Mauritians, then two thirds of the population, elected nobody.
statusPeriods.note: Slavery was abolished on 1 February 1835 and 66,343 people were freed. Britain paid Mauritian slave-owners just over £2 million in compensation. The people freed received nothing, and most left the estates.

statusPeriods.label: Elections widen, slowly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1947 constitution let anyone literate in any language vote, which multiplied the electorate roughly twelvefold at a stroke; the governor still appointed the executive, and full universal suffrage came only in 1958.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Louis, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: From 1948 all adults who could sign their name in any language could vote - about 72,000 people, up from around 6,000. Universal adult suffrage followed in 1958.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Ramgoolam
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The election of 7 August 1967 was fought as a referendum on independence: Ramgoolam's alliance won 55% of the vote and 39 of 62 seats, and formed the government that took the island to independence seven months later.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Mauritius became independent by negotiation after an election fought on the question, three years after Britain had detached the Chagos Archipelago as a condition of the settlement, and two months after communal riots in Port Louis had killed about 25 people.

led.name: Seewoosagur Ramgoolam
led.role: leader of the Labour Party and first prime minister; a doctor who built the independence coalition from the Indo-Mauritian majority

led.name: Gaetan Duval
led.role: leader of the PMSD, which campaigned to stay associated with Britain and won 44% of the vote

led.name: Sookdeo Bissoondoyal
led.role: leader of the Independent Forward Bloc; organised the rural Indo-Mauritian vote for independence

led.name: Abdool Razack Mohamed
led.role: leader of the Comite d'Action Musulman, whose support made the independence majority

departures.movement: Mauritius Labour Party and its independence alliance

cost.note: The communal riots in Port Louis in January 1968 killed about 25 people; British troops were flown in to restore order. Independence itself was peaceful. The much larger cost was borne by the Chagossians, who were not Mauritian voters and whose removal was the price of the settlement.

departures.borders: Mauritius became independent minus a third of its territory. Britain detached the Chagos Archipelago on 8 November 1965, and Mauritian ministers said afterwards that they had been told independence depended on agreeing. The ICJ found in 2019 that this made the decolonisation of Mauritius incomplete.

instrument.name: Mauritius Independence Act 1968

contested.note: Whether Mauritius consented to the detachment of the Chagos is disputed. British records show ministers agreeing at Lancaster House in September 1965; Mauritian leaders, and the ICJ in 2019, treated that agreement as given under duress by a colony that could not yet refuse.

evidence.author: Philippe Sands
evidence.work: The Last Colony: A Tale of Exile, Justice and Britain's Colonial Legacy
evidence.supports: The 1965 detachment, the independence bargain and the ICJ case.

slavery.note: Britain took Mauritius in 1810 on terms that guaranteed the French planters their property, which meant the people they held as property; the island then became a centre of illegal slave trading, with an estimated 30,000 people landed after Britain had banned the trade.

abolitionDate.note: The British ban applied to Mauritius from its capture, and was systematically evaded there for two decades.

emancipationDate.note: Followed by four years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' which ended early, in 1839, after resistance.

toll.money: Just over £2 million was paid to Mauritian slave-owners in 1835 as compensation for the loss of 66,343 people. The people themselves received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Estimates of the total number of people trafficked to Mauritius under Dutch, French and British rule range widely; Richard B. Allen's work gives figures in this range, including about 30,000 landed illegally after 1810.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.supports: Just over £2 million was paid to Mauritian slave-owners in 1835 as compensation for the loss of 66,343 people.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1834 and 1910 about 450,000 indentured labourers arrived from India to replace the people just freed; roughly two thirds stayed, and their descendants are the majority of Mauritians today.

toll.note: Figures from the immigration depot registers at Port Louis, now a UNESCO World Heritage site as the Aapravasi Ghat. About a third of arrivals returned to India.

warrant.author: The immigration depot at Port Louis, in its own registers
warrant.work: The indenture registers of the Aapravasi Ghat, Port Louis
warrant.supports: Figures from the immigration depot registers at Port Louis, now a UNESCO World Heritage site as the Aapravasi Ghat. About a third of arrivals returned to India.
warrant.check: Held by the Mauritius National Archives and the Aapravasi Ghat Trust Fund; the depot is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
warrant.note: Indenture was registered because the state wanted to be able to find people. That is why this figure is firmer than almost any other movement of people here.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept the Chagos Archipelago, which had been governed from Port Louis since 1814, and it is the last piece of the British Empire in the Indian Ocean.

commonwealth.note: A realm until it became a republic on 12 March 1992, and a Commonwealth member throughout.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar was 99% of exports at independence and the World Bank predicted disaster; Mauritius instead built textiles, tourism and finance and became one of Africa's highest-income countries.
consequences.languageAndLaw: A French civil code, English criminal procedure, courts that hear appeals in London until 1968 and in the Privy Council afterwards, and a population that speaks Creole at home, French in the papers and English in Parliament.

peak.populationNote: The 1962 census gave 681,619 and the population at independence was about 771,000. In 1835, at emancipation, it was around 100,000.

pedagogy.hook: The day slavery ended in Mauritius, 66,343 people walked free and their former owners were paid £2 million for the loss. Within a year the first ships of Indian indentured labourers were arriving to replace them.

misconception.belief: Abolition in 1833 ended forced labour in the British Empire.
misconception.correction: It changed its legal form. Mauritius was the laboratory: from 1834 the 'Great Experiment' brought about 450,000 Indian workers on five-year contracts, tied to one estate, jailed for absconding under vagrancy laws, and paid about five rupees a month. Historians argue about how close this was to slavery; nobody argues it was free labour.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Mauritius is where the empire tested what came after slavery, and the answer - indenture - was then exported to Guyana, Trinidad, Natal, Fiji and Malaya. It is also the island Britain broke up in 1965 to build an American airbase.

territories.name: Seychelles
territories.formalName: The Colony of Seychelles

modernSuccessors.name: Seychelles
modernSuccessors.note: A republic from independence. James Mancham was overthrown by France-Albert Rene in a coup on 5 June 1977, and Seychelles was a one-party state until 1993.

geoCoverage.label: Inner granitic islands and the coral outer islands
Without Aldabra, Farquhar and Desroches
geoCoverage.change: Britain moved three island groups into the new British Indian Ocean Territory in 1965 to build an airfield on Aldabra; it returned them at independence in 1976.

acquisitions.how: Commodore Henry Newcome's squadron appeared off Mahe and the French commandant, Jean-Baptiste Queau de Quinssy, surrendered the settlement of about 600 people without a shot - the first of seven capitulations he negotiated over the next sixteen years, each time raising the French flag again once the British sailed away.

counterparties.name: Revolutionary France
counterparties.lost: It lost effective control of a young settlement founded in 1770, though its administrator stayed in office throughout and French law and language survived British rule entirely.

counterparties.name: The enslaved population of Seychelles
counterparties.lost: About 500 enslaved Africans and Malagasy, the great majority of the population, changed sovereign seven times without any change in their condition.

instrument.name: Capitulation of the Seychelles to Commodore Henry Newcome

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Queau de Quinssy
people.role: French commandant who surrendered the islands seven times and governed them under British rule until 1827

people.name: Henry Newcome
people.role: British commodore who took the first capitulation

acquisitions.resistance: None. De Quinssy's policy was capitulation and survival; he kept a French and a British flag ready and flew whichever the guns in the harbour required.

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Seychelles Since 1770: History of a Slave and Post-Slavery Society
evidence.supports: The capitulations, de Quinssy's role and the slave society.

acquisitions.how: France ceded the Seychelles with Mauritius at the Treaty of Paris, and Britain governed them as a dependency of Mauritius, 1,750 kilometres away, for the next 89 years.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: It gave up the islands it had settled in 1770, keeping only Reunion in the Indian Ocean.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris, 1814

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Seychelles Since 1770: History of a Slave and Post-Slavery Society
evidence.supports: The cession and the Mauritius dependency.

statusPeriods.label: Seven capitulations and a French administrator
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain took the islands' surrender repeatedly and never garrisoned them; de Quinssy went on governing under both flags until Captain Philip Beaver installed a British civil agent in April 1811.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Almost nothing: the French administrator remained in office, French law applied, and no British official lived there for seventeen years after the first capitulation.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Mahe, in practice by the French commandant
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Most of the population was enslaved.

statusPeriods.label: A dependency of Mauritius
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Seychelles was governed as an outlying district of Mauritius by a civil agent and later a Chief Civil Commissioner; laws made in Port Louis applied, and appeals went there.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Victoria, under the Governor of Mauritius
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1861 and 1874 the Royal Navy landed about 2,500 Africans freed from slave ships intercepted off East Africa; they were 'apprenticed' to Seychelles plantations for terms of years and their descendants are a large part of the population.

statusPeriods.label: A Crown Colony in its own right
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor in Victoria answered to the Colonial Office. Seychelles was also the empire's remote prison for inconvenient rulers: Prempeh I of Asante, Saad Zaghloul of Egypt, Kabaka Mutesa II of Buganda and Archbishop Makarios III of Cyprus were all exiled here.
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise elected a minority of the Legislative Council from 1948, when about 2,000 people out of 34,000 could vote. Universal adult suffrage came in 1967.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A coalition of Mancham's Democratic Party and Rene's People's United Party governed internally while Britain retained defence and external affairs for nine months.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Seychelles became independent by negotiation, and Britain returned Aldabra, Farquhar and Desroches at the same moment - the only territory Britain has ever handed back out of the British Indian Ocean Territory.

led.name: James Mancham
led.role: leader of the Democratic Party, who wanted Seychelles to stay British, and became first president anyway

led.name: France-Albert Rene
led.role: leader of the People's United Party, who campaigned for independence, became prime minister, and seized power in June 1977

led.name: Colin Hamilton Allan
led.role: last British governor

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. Rene's coup eleven months later killed one or two people and installed a one-party state that lasted until 1993.

departures.borders: Britain gave back the three island groups it had taken in 1965 and kept the Chagos, 1,700 kilometres to the east. The difference: Aldabra's people were giant tortoises and seabirds, and a scientific campaign saved the island; Chagos had a human population, and it was removed.

instrument.name: Seychelles Act 1976

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Seychelles Since 1770: History of a Slave and Post-Slavery Society
evidence.supports: The road to independence and the 1977 coup.

slavery.note: Seychelles was a slave society: at emancipation in 1835 about 6,500 enslaved people were freed on a total population of roughly 8,500, and their owners were compensated.

toll.note: Colonial registers give about 6,500 people freed in 1835. Estimates of the total trafficked to the islands from 1770 are less certain.

consequences.economicLegacy: Coconut oil, cinnamon and vanilla until the airport opened in 1971; tourism and fishing licences afterwards. Seychelles now has the highest income per head in Africa.

peak.populationNote: The 1977 census gave 61,898. In 1830 the population was about 8,500, most of it enslaved.

populationWarrant.supports: Seychelles’s largest recorded population: 61,000 people, counted in 1976.

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr

evidence.supports: The whole span from French settlement to independence.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich

pedagogy.hook: The French governor of Seychelles surrendered to the Royal Navy seven times between 1794 and 1810, and kept his job through all of it by hoisting whichever flag was pointing guns at him.

misconception.belief: Colonies were conquered once and then ruled by the conquerors.
misconception.correction: In Seychelles the conquest took sixteen years, the French administrator stayed in office for thirty-three, and French law, the Catholic church and the language survived British rule entirely. Colonial power often ran through the people who were already there.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Seychelles was the empire's remote prison - Prempeh I of Asante, Saad Zaghloul of Egypt, Kabaka Mutesa II and Archbishop Makarios of Cyprus were all exiled here - which makes it a map of where else Britain was having trouble.

territories.name: Maldives
territories.formalName: The Maldive Islands, a British protected state

modernSuccessors.name: Maldives
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 11 November 1968, when a referendum abolished the sultanate that had lasted more than eight centuries.

acquisitions.how: When Britain took Colombo from the Dutch the Maldives' customary tribute to the governor of Ceylon transferred with it, and the sultanate found itself the client of a new power it had never dealt with.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company
counterparties.lost: It lost the tribute in cowries and coir that the Maldive sultans had sent to Colombo since the 1650s, along with Ceylon itself.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of the Maldives
counterparties.lost: Nothing immediately - the sultans kept full internal power - but the relationship set the pattern that became a protectorate in 1887.

evidence.author: Clarence Maloney
evidence.work: People of the Maldive Islands
evidence.supports: The Maldives' tributary relationship with Colombo and its transfer to Britain.

acquisitions.how: Sultan Muhammad Mueenuddeen II signed an agreement with the Governor of Ceylon accepting British protection and giving up the right to deal with any foreign power, in exchange for internal self-rule and a guarantee against invasion.

counterparties.name: Sultan Muhammad Mueenuddeen II
counterparties.lost: He gave up all foreign relations and the right to lease any part of the islands to another state; he kept complete control of everything inside them, which is the deal he wanted.

counterparties.name: The Borah merchants of Bombay and their rivals
counterparties.lost: The agreement came out of a commercial quarrel in Male in which British Indian subjects were killed; the protectorate settled who would adjudicate such disputes in future.
counterparties.note: The 1887 agreement followed years of instability in which Indian merchant houses backed rival claimants to the throne.

instrument.name: Agreement between the Sultan of the Maldive Islands and the Governor of Ceylon

people.name: Muhammad Mueenuddeen II
people.role: Sultan who signed the protectorate agreement

people.name: Arthur Havelock
people.role: Governor of Ceylon who negotiated it

acquisitions.resistance: None to the agreement itself. Resistance came in 1959, when the three southern atlas atolls seceded, and in 1962, when Male reasserted control.

evidence.author: Clarence Maloney
evidence.work: People of the Maldive Islands
evidence.supports: The 1887 agreement and its terms.

statusPeriods.label: Tribute to Colombo
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The sultans ruled and sent an annual present to the British governor of Ceylon. No British official visited for decades at a time.
statusPeriods.franchise: None; the sultanate was elective within a narrow group of families.

statusPeriods.label: Protected state administered through Ceylon
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain handled the Maldives' foreign relations through the Governor of Ceylon and did nothing else: it collected no tax, appointed no official and kept no garrison. The sultan, and from 1932 a constitution and a majlis, ran everything internal.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Male, with British business handled at Colombo
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1932 constitution created a majlis chosen by a mixture of appointment and limited election - the first written constitution in Maldivian history, and unpopular enough to be publicly burned.

statusPeriods.label: Direct with London, and the base at Gan
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ceylon's independence in 1948 forced a new agreement direct with Britain. In 1956-57 Britain took a 100-year lease on Gan in Addu Atoll for an RAF staging base, evacuating the island's roughly 700 inhabitants to neighbouring islands.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Male, with a British representative at Colombo and an RAF station at Gan
statusPeriods.franchise: A majlis with limited elections. The republic of 1953 lasted seven months before the sultanate was restored.
statusPeriods.note: In 1959 the three southern atolls, which had the base and the wages, seceded as the United Suvadive Republic under Abdullah Afeef. Britain declined to recognise it but dealt with it in practice for three years; Male crushed it in 1962-63 and Afeef was evacuated by the Royal Navy to Seychelles, where he died in 1993.

departures.how: Ibrahim Nasir and the British High Commissioner signed independence into effect at Colombo, with a separate agreement letting Britain keep the airfield at Gan; the RAF stayed eleven more years and left in 1976.

led.name: Ibrahim Nasir
led.role: prime minister who negotiated independence and became president in 1968

led.name: Abdullah Afeef
led.role: led the southern atolls' secession of 1959-63 against Male's control of the Gan wages; exiled to Seychelles

led.name: Michael Walker
led.role: British High Commissioner in Ceylon who signed the independence agreement

departures.movement: Maldivian nationalist opinion in Male and the majlis

cost.note: Independence was peaceful. The suppression of the Suvadive secession in 1962-63 involved gunboats and burned villages in Havaru Thinadhoo, whose population was deported and the island left empty for four years; no reliable death toll exists.

departures.borders: The Maldives kept every atoll, including the southern three that had tried to leave. Gan stayed British by lease until 1976, so a foreign airbase sat inside an independent country for eleven years.

instrument.name: Agreement on independence between the United Kingdom and the Maldive Islands, signed at Colombo

evidence.author: J. J. Robinson
evidence.work: The Maldives: Islamic Republic, Tropical Autocracy
evidence.supports: Independence, the Gan base and the Suvadive secession.

violence.note: Male's suppression of the southern secession in 1962-63 emptied the island of Havaru Thinadhoo for four years; Britain, which had encouraged the southerners informally and then abandoned them, did nothing.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept the RAF base on Gan under a separate lease until 31 March 1976, eleven years after Maldivian independence.

commonwealth.note: Joined as a special member in 1982, became a full member in 1985, left in 2016 over criticism of its human rights record, and rejoined in 2020.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Maldives lived on dried tuna and cowrie shells under British protection and had no tourism at all until 1972; the first resort opened seven years after independence.

peak.populationNote: The 1967 census gave 103,801; the 1965 figure is an estimate. In 1911 the population was about 72,000.

evidence.author: Clarence Maloney
evidence.work: People of the Maldive Islands
evidence.supports: Maldivian society and the protectorate relationship.

evidence.author: J. J. Robinson
evidence.work: The Maldives: Islamic Republic, Tropical Autocracy
evidence.supports: The twentieth-century political history, Gan and independence.

pedagogy.hook: The Maldives were British for 78 years without a single British official, tax or soldier - until Britain wanted an airfield in 1957 and moved 700 people off their island to get it.

misconception.belief: Being in the British Empire meant being governed by Britain.
misconception.correction: In the Maldives it meant almost nothing for 70 years: the sultan governed, Britain handled foreign relations, and no British administrator lived in the country. Then Britain wanted a base, and the relationship suddenly had teeth. Protection was cheap until it needed to be cashed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Gan explains the whole Indian Ocean story in miniature: a base needs an island, an island has people, and the people get moved. Ten years later the same logic emptied Diego Garcia, 700 kilometres to the south.

territories.name: British Indian Ocean Territory
territories.formalName: The British Indian Ocean Territory (the Chagos Archipelago, with Diego Garcia)

namesOverTime.name: The Oil Islands

from.note: A working name from the coconut-oil trade; the plantations date from French settlement in the 1780s and 1790s.

namesOverTime.note: Governed as the Lesser Dependencies of Mauritius; the coconut-oil and copra plantations ran continuously for about 180 years.

namesOverTime.name: Chagos Archipelago
namesOverTime.note: The name Mauritius and the ICJ use. What you call it is an argument about who owns it.

modernSuccessors.name: Mauritius
modernSuccessors.note: The UK and Mauritius signed a treaty on 22 May 2025 transferring sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius while leasing Diego Garcia back for 99 years. Confirm its entry into force before treating the transfer as complete.

geoCoverage.label: Chagos plus Aldabra, Farquhar and Desroches
The Chagos Archipelago alone
geoCoverage.change: The three Seychelles island groups went back at Seychelles independence in 1976, leaving BIOT as the Chagos Archipelago: 55 islands, one airbase and no permitted inhabitants.

acquisitions.how: An Order in Council cut the Chagos Archipelago out of Mauritius and three island groups out of Seychelles to make a new colony with no purpose but to host American bases, three years before Mauritius became independent.

counterparties.name: Mauritius
counterparties.lost: It lost 60 islands and about 15,000 square kilometres of the territory it was about to become independent with, for £3 million and a promise of fishing and mineral rights. The ICJ found in 2019 that this was not a free choice.
counterparties.note: Mauritian ministers were told at Lancaster House in September 1965 that independence and the detachment were linked.

counterparties.name: Seychelles
counterparties.lost: It lost Aldabra, Farquhar and Desroches for eleven years, and got them back at independence in 1976.

counterparties.name: The Chagossians (Ilois)
counterparties.lost: They lost their homes, their work, their graves and their nationality. Between 1,500 and 2,000 people, born on the islands over five or six generations, were removed between 1967 and 1973 and never allowed back.

instrument.name: British Indian Ocean Territory Order 1965
instrument.note: Followed by the UK-US Exchange of Notes of 30 December 1966, which made the islands available to the United States for 50 years with a 20-year extension. The United States contributed about $14 million through a secret discount on Polaris missiles, so that no payment appeared in either country's accounts.

people.name: Harold Wilson
people.role: prime minister who authorised the detachment and, according to his own official's note, warned the Mauritian premier he could be 'frightened' into agreeing

people.name: Seewoosagur Ramgoolam
people.role: Mauritian premier who agreed to the detachment at Lancaster House in September 1965 and spent the rest of his life saying he had no choice

people.name: Denis Greenhill
people.role: Foreign Office official whose 1966 minute described the islanders as 'some few Tarzans or Man Fridays whose origins are obscure'

people.name: Bruce Greatbatch
people.role: Governor of Seychelles and BIOT Commissioner, who ordered the Chagossians' dogs destroyed in 1971 to make clear the islands were closing

cost.money: Britain paid Mauritius £3 million for the archipelago in 1965 and £650,000 in 1973 as compensation for the Chagossians, which reached them slowly and partially. A further £4 million with a Mauritian contribution followed in 1982.
cost.note: The number removed is usually given as between 1,500 and 2,000. Exact figures are disputed because the plantation registers counted contract workers and residents differently, and because people who left temporarily for medical treatment in Mauritius were simply refused return.

warrant.author: The Chagos plantation registers, and the British and Mauritian counts made afterwards
warrant.work: Plantation registers of the Chagos Archipelago and the removal records of 1965–73
warrant.supports: The number removed is usually given as between 1,500 and 2,000. Exact figures are disputed because the plantation registers counted contract workers and residents differently, and because people who left temporarily for medical treatment in Mauritius were simply refused return.
warrant.check: FCO 31 and CO 1036 at The National Archives, Kew, and the evidence rehearsed in the Bancoult judgments.
warrant.note: The registers counted contract workers and residents differently, and people away for medical treatment were simply not counted back. The dispute over the number is a dispute about who was a resident.

acquisitions.resistance: Chagossians have fought in court since 1975: the Vencatessen case, Bancoult (No 1) in 2000 which found the removal unlawful, the 2004 Orders in Council that overturned it, Bancoult (No 2) in the House of Lords in 2008, and the ICJ opinion of 2019. Olivier Bancoult has led the Chagos Refugees Group since 1983.

evidence.author: David Vine
evidence.work: Island of Shame: The Secret History of the U.S. Military Base on Diego Garcia
evidence.supports: The creation of BIOT, the UK-US deal and the removal of the Chagossians.

statusPeriods.label: A colony created to be emptied
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Commissioner sitting in London governed by ordinance. Immigration Ordinance No. 1 of 1971 made it unlawful for anyone to be on the islands without a permit, which is the legal instrument by which a population was removed from its own country.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: London, through the BIOT Commissioner and Administrator
statusPeriods.franchise: None. There has never been an election in the British Indian Ocean Territory.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory, population zero
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Still governed by a Commissioner in London and still closed. Diego Garcia holds a US base of some 2,500 to 4,000 military personnel and contractors; the other 54 islands are empty and a 640,000-square-kilometre Marine Protected Area, declared in 2010, was ruled unlawful by an arbitral tribunal in 2015.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the usual 3 for an overseas territory: BIOT has no inhabitants with rights, no legislature and no local government at all, so British authority is total.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: A leaked 2009 US diplomatic cable recorded a British official saying the marine reserve would make resettlement impossible - the ground on which the tribunal later found the declaration procedurally unlawful.

departures.how: Aldabra, Farquhar and Desroches went back to Seychelles at its independence, because the airfield Britain had planned for Aldabra was cancelled in 1967 after a scientific campaign to save the atoll's giant tortoises.

led.name: France-Albert Rene
led.role: Seychelles prime minister who pressed for the islands' return

led.name: Solly Zuckerman
led.role: British chief scientific adviser whose review helped kill the Aldabra airfield in 1967

cost.note: Nobody was removed from Aldabra: it had no permanent human population, only a research station and the largest population of giant tortoises on earth.

departures.borders: The return left BIOT as the Chagos Archipelago alone. Aldabra is now a UNESCO World Heritage site; Diego Garcia is a runway, a harbour and a listening station.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The Aldabra decision and the 1976 return.

departures.how: Britain still administers the Chagos Archipelago, sixty years after taking it and six years after the International Court of Justice said it should end that administration as rapidly as possible; a treaty signed with Mauritius on 22 May 2025 would transfer sovereignty and lease Diego Garcia back for 99 years.

led.name: Olivier Bancoult
led.role: leader of the Chagos Refugees Group since 1983 and lead claimant in the British court cases

led.name: Philippe Sands
led.role: counsel for Mauritius at the International Court of Justice in 2018-19

led.name: Marie Liseby Elyse
led.role: Chagossian who gave evidence to the ICJ describing her removal from Peros Banhos while pregnant

cost.note: No Chagossian has been allowed to live on the islands since 1973. Many died in poverty in Mauritius and Seychelles; a British Home Office scheme offered citizenship to their descendants from 2002 and again in 2022.

departures.borders: Mauritius has claimed the archipelago since 1968. The ICJ advised in 2019 that Britain's continued administration is an unlawful act, and the UN General Assembly agreed by 116 votes to 6.

contested.note: The legal status of the Chagos is genuinely unsettled at the time of writing. The ICJ opinion of 2019 is advisory, not binding; the UK long rejected it; the 2025 treaty would end the dispute but its entry into force depends on ratification and implementing legislation. Check the current position before stating that Britain has left.

evidence.author: Philippe Sands
evidence.work: The Last Colony: A Tale of Exile, Justice and Britain's Colonial Legacy
evidence.supports: The litigation, the ICJ opinion and the Chagossian case.

stillBritish.note: The Chagos Archipelago remains a British Overseas Territory with no civilian population, pending the entry into force of the treaty signed with Mauritius on 22 May 2025.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1967 and 1973 the whole population was removed: people away for medical treatment in Mauritius were told they could not return, the copra plantations were closed, and the last families were shipped out of Peros Banhos in May 1973.

toll.note: Estimates vary because plantation registers distinguished contract workers from residents; the descendant community now numbers about 10,000 in Mauritius, Seychelles and the UK.

violence.note: There was no shooting. There was an immigration ordinance, a closed supply ship, and in 1971 the killing of about 800 pet dogs on Diego Garcia, gassed and burned in a copra drying shed while their owners watched.

consequences.borderLegacy: A colony was created in 1965 out of two other colonies specifically so that it could be kept when they became independent - the clearest case in the empire of a border drawn to defeat decolonisation.

peak.populationNote: About 1,000 people lived on Diego Garcia and roughly 500 more on Peros Banhos and Salomon in the mid-1960s. Land area is about 60 square kilometres across 55 islands, in an ocean territory of 640,000 square kilometres.

evidence.author: David Vine
evidence.work: Island of Shame: The Secret History of the U.S. Military Base on Diego Garcia
evidence.supports: The base, the removal and the documents behind both.

evidence.author: Philippe Sands
evidence.work: The Last Colony: A Tale of Exile, Justice and Britain's Colonial Legacy
evidence.supports: The ICJ case and the Chagossians' legal struggle.

evidence.author: Stephen Allen
evidence.work: The Chagos Islanders and International Law
evidence.supports: The legal analysis of the detachment, the removal and the litigation.

contested.note: Britain long maintained that the islands had no permanent population, only a transient contract workforce, and that Mauritius consented to the detachment in 1965. The ICJ in 2019 and the UK courts in 2000 rejected both propositions; the 2025 treaty effectively concedes the sovereignty point.

pedagogy.hook: Britain created a colony in 1965 for the sole purpose of removing everybody from it, and an official described the people who lived there as 'some few Tarzans or Man Fridays whose origins are obscure'.

misconception.belief: The British Empire ended with decolonisation in the 1960s.
misconception.correction: In 1965, in the middle of decolonisation, Britain made a brand-new colony. It cut the Chagos out of Mauritius three years before Mauritian independence precisely so it could keep them, removed the population between 1967 and 1973, and still administers the islands sixty years later.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Chagos is the case where the empire's last chapter is still being written, in courtrooms. It also shows what decolonisation left out: the ICJ said in 2019 that a colony cannot be split up before independence, which means the empire's rules were broken by the empire itself, in living memory.
