Immigration Ordinance No. 1 makes it illegal to live there
The last Chagossians are deported from Peros Banhos
The ICJ finds Britain's administration unlawful
UK and Mauritius sign a treaty transferring sovereignty

territories.name: Christmas Island
territories.formalName: Christmas Island, a dependency of the Straits Settlements and then of Singapore

modernSuccessors.name: Australia
modernSuccessors.note: An Australian external territory. Its immigration detention centre, opened in 2001, made it the focus of Australia's offshore asylum policy.

acquisitions.how: Britain annexed the uninhabited island after a naturalist's rock samples proved it was almost solid phosphate, and granted a 99-year lease to a company founded by John Murray and George Clunies-Ross of the Cocos Islands.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Christmas Island had never been permanently inhabited: it is a limestone plateau with no fresh surface water and a difficult landing.

people.name: John Murray
people.role: Challenger expedition naturalist whose analysis of the island's rock led directly to its annexation

people.name: George Clunies-Ross
people.role: of the Cocos Islands; co-founder of the phosphate company and the island's first settler-employer

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The annexation, the phosphate lease and the transfer to Australia.

statusPeriods.label: A company island under Singapore
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Formally attached to the Straits Settlements from 1900, the island was in practice run by the Christmas Island Phosphate Company, which owned the housing, the shop, the railway and the labour contracts of its Chinese and Malay workforce.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Indentured Chinese workers, recruited from Singapore and Guangdong, mined the phosphate under contracts they could not leave; mortality in the early years was very high.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Indian gunners of the garrison mutinied on the night of 10 March 1942, killed five British soldiers and imprisoned the rest, and the island surrendered to a Japanese force on 31 March. Japan deported most of the workforce to Java; about 850 people remained.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was extinguished for three and a half years; the island was administered by Japan.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Part of the Colony of Singapore
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain resumed control and attached the island to Singapore in 1946. The phosphate company was bought out in 1949 by the Australian and New Zealand governments, which then wanted the island itself.
statusPeriods.franchise: None on the island.

departures.how: Britain transferred the island to Australia, which paid Singapore about £2.9 million in compensation for the phosphate revenue it would lose - the island and its 2,600 people were sold between two governments without anyone asking them.

led.name: Lim Yew Hock
led.role: Chief Minister of Singapore, whose government was compensated for the loss of the island's phosphate royalties

led.name: Robert Menzies
led.role: Australian prime minister whose government wanted the phosphate for Australian farms

cost.note: No one died. The Chinese and Malay workers, most of them born on the island or in Singapore, received Australian residence but not citizenship, and equal pay only in 1980 after a long union campaign.

departures.borders: Christmas Island is 350 kilometres from Java and 1,550 from the Australian mainland. It is Australian because of phosphate and a payment to Singapore, not because of geography.

instrument.name: Christmas Island Act 1958 (Australia) and the Christmas Island Act 1958 (UK)

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The transfer and the compensation paid to Singapore.

populationTransfer.note: The island's whole population was imported: indentured Chinese miners, Malay labourers and Sikh police, brought in from the 1890s to dig phosphate for Australian and Malayan farms.

consequences.economicLegacy: About 30 million tonnes of phosphate had been shipped out by the 1980s, much of it to Australian and New Zealand farms at below world prices, and the mined-out plateau is still being rehabilitated.
consequences.borderLegacy: A British transfer put an island in sight of Java under Australian law, which is why it became the centre of Australia's offshore asylum system a century after annexation.

peak.populationNote: About 2,600 at the transfer, roughly two thirds Chinese, with Malay and Indian minorities and a small European staff. Before 1888 nobody lived there at all.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: Christmas Island's colonial history and transfer.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Singapore, 1819-1975
evidence.supports: The Straits Settlements administration of the island.

pedagogy.hook: Britain annexed this uninhabited island in 1888 because a scientist proved it was made of fertiliser, then sold it to Australia in 1958 for £2.9 million paid to Singapore.

misconception.belief: Colonies were taken for land, settlers or strategic position.
misconception.correction: Some were taken for a mineral. Christmas Island had no people, no harbour and no strategic value; it had phosphate. Britain annexed it after a rock sample was analysed in Edinburgh, and imported an entire indentured population to dig it out.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how empire and commodity chains fused: British annexation, Chinese indentured labour, and phosphate shipped to Australian and New Zealand farms. And it shows decolonisation that was not decolonisation - the island's people simply changed owner in 1958.

keyDates.what: Britain annexes the island for its phosphate
Phosphate mining begins with indentured Chinese labour
Japanese occupation after a mutiny in the garrison
Transferred to Australia for a payment to Singapore

territories.name: Cocos (Keeling) Islands
territories.formalName: The Cocos or Keeling Islands

modernSuccessors.name: Australia
modernSuccessors.note: An Australian external territory. The Cocos Malays voted for integration with Australia in a UN-supervised act of self-determination on 6 April 1984.

acquisitions.how: Captain Stephen Fremantle of HMS Juno annexed the atolls to the British Crown, thirty years after the Scottish trader John Clunies-Ross and the adventurer Alexander Hare had settled them with Malay workers Hare had brought from Java and Borneo.

counterparties.name: No prior population
counterparties.note: The atolls were uninhabited before 1826. Everyone on them descended from the Malay, Javanese, Papuan, Chinese, Indian and South African people Hare and Clunies-Ross brought there, many of them enslaved or bonded.

counterparties.name: The Cocos Malay community
counterparties.lost: They gained a British Crown that then handed the islands to the Clunies-Ross family in perpetuity, so annexation changed nothing: they were paid in company tokens redeemable only at the family store until the 1970s.

people.name: John Clunies-Ross
people.role: Shetland-born trader who settled the atolls in 1827 and founded a family that ruled them for 151 years

people.name: Alexander Hare
people.role: former British official in Java who settled Cocos in 1826 with a household of women and workers he had brought from Borneo; driven off by Clunies-Ross

contested.note: A persistent story says Fremantle was sent to annex a different Cocos group and claimed the wrong islands. Britain's instructions were certainly vague and the annexation had to be confirmed later, but the 'wrong island' version is not well documented and should be treated as a story about administrative confusion rather than an established fact.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The annexation, the Clunies-Ross regime and the 1984 act of self-determination.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed and ignored
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nominally attached to Ceylon and then to the Straits Settlements, the atolls were governed entirely by the Clunies-Ross family; no British official lived there.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Far below the 5 a crown colony implies: Britain claimed sovereignty and exercised none, leaving one family to govern.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: A family estate under the Crown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Queen Victoria granted the islands in perpetuity to George Clunies-Ross and his heirs on 7 July 1886. The family owned every island and was the Cocos Malay people's employer, landlord, shopkeeper and magistrate; it paid wages in 'Cocos rupees', tokens of plastic and ivory valid only in its own store. A United Nations visiting mission in 1974 called the system feudal.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Sovereignty without administration: the Crown's writ ran through a private owner for 69 years.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: Cocos Malay workers petitioned from the 1940s. Australian and UN pressure ended the family's rule: John Cecil Clunies-Ross sold his rights to Australia in 1978 for A$6.25 million, and the islanders voted for integration with Australia in 1984. No new land was taken in 1886 - Britain already held the islands - which is why this is a change of status here and not a fresh taking.

departures.how: Britain transferred the islands to Australia, which wanted the wartime airstrip on West Island as a staging point on the Perth-Colombo air route; the Clunies-Ross family kept its property and its rule for another 23 years.

led.name: John Cecil Clunies-Ross
led.role: owner-ruler at the transfer; his rights were bought out by Australia in 1978

led.name: Parson bin Yapat
led.role: Cocos Malay leader who pressed Australia and the UN for the end of family rule and led the community to the 1984 vote

cost.note: Nobody died. The Cocos Malays were not consulted in 1955; they were consulted in 1984 and chose integration with Australia over independence or free association, by 88 votes to 9 with 24 for free association.

departures.borders: The atolls are 2,750 kilometres from Perth and 1,000 from Java. They are Australian because Australia wanted an airstrip, and Britain no longer wanted the islands.

instrument.name: Cocos Islands Act 1955 (Australia)

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The 1955 transfer and the 1984 act of self-determination.

populationTransfer.note: Every Cocos Malay is descended from people Alexander Hare and John Clunies-Ross brought to uninhabited atolls in 1826-27 from Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Bali, Malacca, Papua, China, India and the Cape - some enslaved, some bonded, none asked.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra was the only industry and the company store the only shop; wages were paid in Cocos rupees until the 1970s and Australia had to buy the islands from their owner in 1978 to end the system.

commonwealth.note: Part of Australia, so a Commonwealth territory without being a member.

peak.populationNote: About 600 Cocos Malays and a handful of Europeans at the transfer. The population is around 550 today.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The Clunies-Ross regime, the transfer and decolonisation.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Singapore, 1819-1975
evidence.supports: The Straits Settlements administration of the islands.

pedagogy.hook: Queen Victoria gave these islands to a Scottish family in 1886, for ever. Their descendants ruled them, paid the workers in tokens spendable only at the family shop, and were finally bought out by Australia in 1978.

misconception.belief: The empire was governed by officials answering to Parliament.
misconception.correction: Sometimes it was governed by a private family with a royal grant. On Cocos the Clunies-Rosses owned the land, the boats, the store and the currency for 121 years, and a UN mission in 1974 called the arrangement feudal. Sovereignty and government were not the same thing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cocos is the clearest surviving example of proprietary empire - the model that also produced the Barbados of the 1620s and the chartered companies of Africa. It ended not with independence but with a purchase and a UN-supervised vote in 1984.

keyDates.what: John Clunies-Ross settles the atolls with Malay workers
Britain annexes the islands
Victoria grants them to the Clunies-Ross family in perpetuity
Transferred to Australia
The Cocos Malays vote to integrate with Australia

territories.name: Heard and McDonald Islands
territories.formalName: Heard Island and the McDonald Islands

modernSuccessors.name: Australia
modernSuccessors.note: An Australian external territory and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997, with no permanent inhabitants and Australia's only active volcano.

geoCoverage.label: Ice, rock and an active volcano

acquisitions.how: Britain formally asserted sovereignty over the islands, resting the claim on their sighting by British and American captains in the 1850s and on three decades of sealing from them, and then did nothing with them for 37 years.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Heard Island is 4,100 kilometres south-west of Perth, ice-covered, and has never had a permanent human population. Its only settlements have been sealing camps and research stations.

counterparties.name: The elephant seal and penguin colonies
counterparties.lost: American and British sealers killed an estimated 100,000 elephant seals here between 1855 and the 1880s, boiling them for oil until the population collapsed and the trade with it.

contested.note: The date and instrument of the British claim are not well documented in accessible sources. Sovereignty was asserted in the early twentieth century and is usually given as 1910, but the claim was consolidated only by the Australian landing of 1947 and Australian legislation in 1953. Treat 1910 as approximate.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The sub-Antarctic claims and their transfer to Australia.

statusPeriods.label: A claim on a chart
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed. British sovereignty over Heard and the McDonalds was a line in the Admiralty's records and a paragraph in the Colonial Office List; no official, garrison or resident ever went there under British rule.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Almost none: sovereignty asserted over uninhabited islands with no administration of any kind for 37 years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere in practice; London on paper
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody lived there.

departures.how: An Australian National Antarctic Research Expedition landed at Atlas Cove on 26 December 1947 and raised the flag; Britain agreed the transfer and Australia legislated for the islands in 1953.

becomes.name: Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands, Australia

led.name: Stuart Campbell
led.role: Australian expedition leader who landed at Atlas Cove and took over the islands

led.name: Douglas Mawson
led.role: Antarctic explorer whose surveys underpinned Australia's southern territorial claims; Mawson Peak on Heard is named after him

cost.note: Nobody lived there and nobody was displaced. The cost had been paid earlier, by roughly 100,000 elephant seals killed for oil in the sealing decades.

departures.borders: The transfer was part of a wider handover of southern claims: Australia took Heard, the McDonalds and the Australian Antarctic Territory, and the sub-Antarctic map of the Indian Ocean was redrawn between two governments with no population to consult.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The transfer of the sub-Antarctic islands to Australia.

consequences.economicLegacy: The only industry the islands ever had was sealing, and it destroyed its own resource within thirty years; there has been no commercial activity since, only research and a licensed fishery in surrounding waters.
consequences.borderLegacy: Heard's transfer helped anchor Australia's claim to 42% of Antarctica, which most of the world does not recognise.

peak.populationNote: No permanent population has ever lived on Heard or the McDonald Islands. Sealing gangs wintered there in the 1850s to 1870s, sometimes over 200 men at a time.

evidence.author: Robert Aldrich
evidence.work: The Last Colonies
evidence.supports: The status and transfer of the sub-Antarctic islands.

contested.note: This is the thinnest-documented entry in the region. The date and legal basis of the original British claim are uncertain in accessible sources, and the transfer to Australia is better recorded than the taking. The 1947 flag-raising is firm; 1910 is approximate.

pedagogy.hook: Britain claimed these islands around 1910 and never sent a single official. The claim was made real 37 years later by Australians landing on Boxing Day 1947 and putting up a flag.

misconception.belief: Territory belonged to whoever discovered it.
misconception.correction: Under the law empires used, a claim had to be occupied to be secure. Britain's paper claim to Heard was worth little until someone lived there, which is why Australia's 1947 expedition and its 1953 statute matter more than any nineteenth-century sighting.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire at its emptiest: a possession with no people, no government and no economy after the seals were gone, held for four decades because a line on a chart was cheap.

keyDates.what: The American sealer John Heard sights the island
Sealing begins; about 100,000 elephant seals are killed in 30 years
Britain asserts sovereignty
Australians land at Atlas Cove and take over

events.title: The General Maritime Treaty
events.summary: After a Royal Navy and Bombay Marine expedition destroyed the Qawasim fleet and town of Ras al-Khaimah in December 1819, the sheikhs of the lower Gulf signed a treaty banning war and plunder at sea and requiring their ships to fly a flag registered with the British.
events.significance: It is the legal root of everything British in the Gulf: the Trucial States, the Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853, the exclusive agreements of 1892 and the protected states of Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar all descend from it. British power in Arabia began at sea, and was run from Bombay for the next 127 years.

places.name: Ras al-Khaimah
places.note: Destroyed by the British expedition in December 1819.

places.name: Bushire (Bandar Bushehr)
places.note: Seat of the Political Resident in the Persian Gulf, in Persia, from 1822 to 1946.

people.name: William Grant Keir
people.role: commanded the 1819 expedition and dictated the treaty

people.name: Hassan bin Rahma Al Qasimi
people.role: sheikh of Ras al-Khaimah who surrendered the town

people.name: Sultan Muhammad Al-Qasimi
people.role: historian and ruler of Sharjah who argued in 1986 that the piracy charge was largely fabricated

toll.note: No reliable count of Arab dead at Ras al-Khaimah exists; British losses were about 5 killed. The range is a modern estimate from the size of the town and the length of the bombardment.

pedagogy.hook: Britain took over the Gulf by defining piracy, then punishing it: the treaty made British registration the only lawful flag an Arab ship could fly.

misconception.belief: Britain suppressed piracy in the Gulf as a neutral service to shipping.
misconception.correction: The Qawasim were the region's largest Arab carriers and allied to the Wahhabis. Destroying their fleet removed a commercial rival as well as a threat, and Gulf historians reading the same East India Company files have argued for forty years that the piracy label was largely a pretext.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how maritime policing became sovereignty: no conquest, no governor, no tax, just control of who may sail.

evidence.author: Sultan Muhammad Al-Qasimi
evidence.work: The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf
evidence.supports: The revisionist reading of the 1819 expedition.

evidence.author: James Onley
evidence.work: The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj: Merchants, Rulers, and the British in the Nineteenth-Century Gulf
evidence.supports: The treaty system and the residency that enforced it.

contested.note: Whether the Qawasim were pirates or a trading power destroyed under a pretext is genuinely argued among historians, and the argument is about the same documents, not different ones.

events.title: The 'Great Experiment': indenture begins
events.summary: Three months after the Abolition Act came into force, the ship Atlas landed the first group of Indian indentured labourers at Port Louis. Over the next 76 years about 450,000 more followed, bound to Mauritian sugar estates on five-year contracts.
events.significance: Mauritius was the laboratory for what replaced slavery across the empire. The system was copied to British Guiana, Trinidad, Natal, Fiji and Malaya, moved well over a million people, and changed the population of a dozen colonies permanently.

places.name: Aapravasi Ghat, Port Louis
places.note: The immigration depot where arrivals were processed; a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2006.

people.name: John Gladstone
people.role: Demerara plantation owner whose 1836 request for Indian labour extended the Mauritius model to the Caribbean; father of the future prime minister

people.name: Anandi and the 'Gladstone coolies'
people.role: among the first Indian indentured workers shipped to the Caribbean under the system trialled in Mauritius

toll.note: Figures from the Port Louis immigration registers. About a third of arrivals returned to India; mortality on the voyage and in the first year on the estates was high but is unevenly recorded.

pedagogy.hook: The first shipload of indentured Indians reached Mauritius nine months after the Abolition Act, and the planters called the system the Great Experiment.

misconception.belief: Abolition ended forced labour in the British Empire in 1833.
misconception.correction: It replaced one legal form with another. Indentured workers were legally free and contractually bound: tied to one estate, prosecuted for absconding, and paid about five rupees a month. Historians argue over how close it was to slavery; none call it free labour.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why there are Indian-descended majorities or large minorities in Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad, Fiji and Suriname today.

evidence.author: Marina Carter
evidence.work: Servants, Sirdars and Settlers: Indians in Mauritius, 1834-1874
evidence.supports: The organisation and scale of the indenture migration.

evidence.author: Richard B. Allen
evidence.work: Slaves, Freedmen and Indentured Laborers in Colonial Mauritius
evidence.supports: The transition from slavery to indenture.

events.title: Disraeli buys the Suez Canal shares
events.summary: Bankrupt and desperate, Khedive Ismail of Egypt sold his 176,602 shares in the Suez Canal Company - about 44% of it - to the British government for £3,976,582. Disraeli borrowed the money from Lionel de Rothschild overnight, without asking Parliament.
events.significance: Britain had opposed the canal's construction and now owned the largest block of it. The shareholding gave London a direct financial stake in Egypt's stability, which led to the bondholders' control of Egyptian finances, the Urabi revolt and the British occupation of Egypt in 1882 - and the whole logic of holding Aden, Cyprus, Palestine and the Gulf.

places.name: Suez Canal, Ismailia
places.note: Opened 17 November 1869; British troops guarded it until 1956.

people.name: Benjamin Disraeli
people.role: prime minister who bought the shares in four days without parliamentary authority

people.name: Isma'il Pasha
people.role: Khedive of Egypt, who sold his shares to service a debt of about £100 million and was deposed by the powers in 1879

people.name: Lionel de Rothschild
people.role: banker who advanced the £4 million on the government's word

people.name: Ferdinand de Lesseps
people.role: French promoter of the canal, which Britain had spent fifteen years opposing

toll.money: £3,976,582 for 176,602 shares, borrowed from N. M. Rothschild & Sons at 2.5% commission. The stake was worth many times that within twenty years and was sold in 1979 for about £22 million.
toll.note: The canal was dug largely by Egyptian forced labour under the corvee in the 1860s; contemporary estimates of deaths run into the tens of thousands and are not reliable.

pedagogy.hook: Disraeli bought nearly half the Suez Canal in four days, with money borrowed from a banker, and told Parliament afterwards.

misconception.belief: Britain built the Suez Canal.
misconception.correction: France built it, against British opposition, with Egyptian forced labour, and opened it in 1869. Britain bought a shareholding six years later from a bankrupt khedive, and occupied Egypt seven years after that to protect the investment.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The canal turned the Middle East into the corridor of empire. Every British possession from Gibraltar to Aden to the Gulf is a link in the chain that protected it.

evidence.author: Elizabeth Monroe
evidence.work: Britain's Moment in the Middle East, 1914-1971
evidence.supports: The strategic logic of the canal in British Middle Eastern policy.

evidence.author: John Darwin
evidence.work: Unfinished Empire: The Global Expansion of Britain
evidence.supports: The canal purchase and the drift into occupying Egypt.

events.title: The McMahon-Hussein correspondence

date.note: Ten letters exchanged over eight months; the crucial one is McMahon's of 24 October 1915. There is no single signing date because there was no treaty, only letters.

events.summary: Britain's High Commissioner in Egypt exchanged ten letters with Sharif Hussein of Mecca, promising support for Arab independence in return for a revolt against the Ottomans - while excluding 'portions of Syria lying to the west of the districts of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo', words argued over ever since.
events.significance: It is the first of the three contradictory British commitments over the same territory, alongside Sykes-Picot in 1916 and the Balfour Declaration in 1917. Whether Palestine was inside or outside the promised area is the oldest live argument in modern Middle Eastern history.

places.name: Mecca
places.note: Sharif Hussein's seat as Emir of Mecca under Ottoman suzerainty.

places.name: Cairo
places.note: Where McMahon wrote the letters as British High Commissioner in Egypt.

people.name: Hussein bin Ali
people.role: Sharif and Emir of Mecca; launched the Arab Revolt and was later driven out of the Hejaz by Ibn Saud

people.name: Henry McMahon
people.role: British High Commissioner in Egypt; wrote the letters and spent the rest of his life insisting Palestine had been excluded

people.name: Abdullah bin Hussein
people.role: Sharif Hussein's son, who opened the correspondence and became Emir of Transjordan

pedagogy.hook: Britain's promise of Arab independence was ten letters, no treaty, and one sentence about districts west of Damascus that people have argued about for over a century.

misconception.belief: Britain made a clear promise of Arab independence and then broke it.
misconception.correction: The promise was deliberately vague, made by letter rather than treaty, and hedged with reservations about French interests and about coastal Syria. Arab negotiators read it as including Palestine; McMahon and the British government said it did not. Both readings can be argued from the text, which is why the argument has lasted.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the origin of the charge of British betrayal that shaped Arab politics for a century, and a lesson in reading a document's exact words.

evidence.author: Eugene Rogan
evidence.work: The Fall of the Ottomans: The Great War in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The correspondence and its ambiguities.

evidence.author: Elizabeth Monroe
evidence.work: Britain's Moment in the Middle East, 1914-1971
evidence.supports: The place of the correspondence in British wartime policy.

contested.note: Whether Palestine fell inside the area promised to Hussein has been argued since 1918. A British committee in 1939 examined the texts and could not agree; its Arab and British members reached opposite conclusions and published both.

events.title: The Sykes-Picot Agreement
events.summary: Mark Sykes for Britain and Francois Georges-Picot for France secretly agreed how to divide Ottoman Asia between them: France would take Lebanon and coastal Syria, Britain Basra and Baghdad, with zones of influence behind each and Palestine placed under an international regime. Russia approved and took eastern Anatolia.
events.significance: It contradicted what Britain had just promised Sharif Hussein, and what it would promise the Zionist movement in 1917. The Bolsheviks published it in November 1917 and the Arab world learned of it from the newspapers. Its zones were not the modern borders, but its logic - two empires bargaining over other people's countries - shaped every settlement that followed.

places.name: Petrograd
places.note: Where the Bolsheviks found and published the secret agreement in November 1917.

people.name: Mark Sykes
people.role: British MP and Middle East adviser; drew the line and died of influenza at the Paris peace conference in 1919

people.name: Francois Georges-Picot
people.role: French diplomat and former consul in Beirut who negotiated France's share

people.name: Leon Trotsky
people.role: Bolshevik commissar who ordered the tsarist secret treaties published, exposing the agreement

pedagogy.hook: Two officials drew a line from Acre to Kirkuk across a map of countries neither had ever governed, and kept it secret until the Bolsheviks found it in the tsar's files.

misconception.belief: Sykes-Picot drew the borders of the modern Middle East.
misconception.correction: It did not. Its zones look nothing like today's states: Mosul was in the French zone, Palestine was to be international, and there was no Jordan, no Lebanon in its present shape and no Israel. The modern borders came from San Remo in 1920, the 1921 Cairo conference, and Anglo-French commissions in the 1920s. Sykes-Picot set the method, not the map.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the classic case of secret diplomacy contradicting public promises, and the reason 'Sykes-Picot' is still a political insult across the region.

evidence.author: James Barr
evidence.work: A Line in the Sand: Britain, France and the Struggle that Shaped the Middle East
evidence.supports: The negotiation, the text and its long consequences.

evidence.author: David Fromkin
evidence.work: A Peace to End All Peace: The Fall of the Ottoman Empire and the Creation of the Modern Middle East
evidence.supports: The wartime bargains and the postwar settlement.

events.title: The siege and surrender of Kut
events.summary: General Charles Townshend's Anglo-Indian division was besieged at Kut-al-Amara on the Tigris for 147 days and surrendered about 13,000 men to the Ottomans on 29 April 1916, after relief attempts had cost 23,000 more casualties and an attempt to buy the garrison's freedom for £2 million had failed.
events.significance: It was the largest surrender of a British-led force since Yorktown in 1781, and it happened four months after Gallipoli was evacuated. The humiliation forced Britain to take Mesopotamia seriously, transfer it from Indian to imperial control, and push on to Baghdad - the road that ended with the mandate.

places.name: Kut-al-Amara
places.note: A bend in the Tigris where the division was trapped for five months.

people.name: Charles Townshend
people.role: British commander who surrendered at Kut and spent the rest of the war in comfortable captivity while his men died

people.name: Khalil Pasha
people.role: Ottoman commander who took the surrender

people.name: T. E. Lawrence
people.role: sent with Aubrey Herbert to offer the Ottomans £2 million for the garrison's release; refused

toll.note: About 13,000 men surrendered. Of roughly 10,500 British and Indian other ranks marched into captivity, some 4,250 died on the march or in Ottoman labour camps. Officers were treated far better than their men, and the death rates differ by an order of magnitude.

pedagogy.hook: Of the 13,000 men who surrendered at Kut, more than a third died in captivity - most of them Indian soldiers, marched hundreds of kilometres across desert.

misconception.belief: The First World War in the Middle East was fought by British soldiers.
misconception.correction: The Mesopotamia campaign was overwhelmingly an Indian Army operation: roughly two thirds of the force at Kut was Indian, paid for from Indian revenue and commanded from Delhi until 1916. The same is true of the Gulf, Aden and East Africa.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Kut explains why Britain ended up ruling Iraq: it could not leave after a defeat like that.

evidence.author: Eugene Rogan
evidence.work: The Fall of the Ottomans: The Great War in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The siege, the surrender and the fate of the prisoners.

events.title: The Arab Revolt
events.summary: Sharif Hussein of Mecca declared a revolt against Ottoman rule, funded by a British subsidy that reached about £220,000 a month and supplied with British and French weapons. His sons Faisal and Abdullah led forces that took Aqaba in July 1917, cut the Hejaz Railway repeatedly, and entered Damascus in October 1918.
events.significance: The revolt tied down Ottoman troops and gave Britain an Arab ally whose claims it then could not honour. Its leaders became the kings of Iraq and Jordan and the losers of Syria and the Hejaz; the promises made to raise it became the grievance that outlived it.

places.name: Aqaba
places.note: Taken from the landward side in July 1917 by Faisal's forces with Lawrence.

places.name: Medina
places.note: The Ottoman garrison held out until January 1919, two months after the armistice.

people.name: Faisal bin Hussein
people.role: field commander of the Northern Army; King of Syria for four months and King of Iraq for twelve years

people.name: Auda abu Tayi
people.role: Howeitat leader whose horsemen made the capture of Aqaba possible

people.name: T. E. Lawrence
people.role: British liaison officer whose account made the revolt famous and overstated his own part in it

people.name: Nuri al-Said
people.role: Ottoman-trained Iraqi officer who joined the revolt and became Iraq's dominant politician

people.name: Hussein bin Ali
people.role: Sharif of Mecca; proclaimed the revolt and lost his kingdom to Ibn Saud in 1925

toll.money: British subsidies to Sharif Hussein reached about £220,000 a month by 1918, alongside rifles, machine guns, gold sovereigns and armoured cars.
toll.note: Casualty figures for the revolt are poor. Ottoman losses in the Hejaz and Transjordan ran into the thousands; Arab irregular losses were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: Britain paid for the Arab Revolt at about £220,000 a month in gold, and then gave its leader's kingdom to France.

misconception.belief: Lawrence of Arabia led the Arab Revolt.
misconception.correction: He was a liaison officer with the Northern Army, one of several, and his own book says so more clearly than the film does. The revolt was commanded by Faisal, Ali and Abdullah bin Hussein, and fought by Bedouin levies of the Hijaz and by Arab officers who had deserted the Ottoman army, such as Nuri al-Said and Jafar al-Askari.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It made the Hashemites Britain's clients and put them on two thrones - and made Britain's broken promises the founding grievance of Arab nationalism.

evidence.author: Eugene Rogan
evidence.work: The Fall of the Ottomans: The Great War in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The course of the revolt and the Arab officers who led it.

evidence.author: Elizabeth Monroe
evidence.work: Britain's Moment in the Middle East, 1914-1971
evidence.supports: British subsidy policy and the revolt's political consequences.

events.title: The Balfour Declaration
events.summary: In 67 words to Lord Rothschild, the Foreign Secretary declared that Britain viewed with favour 'the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people', and that nothing should prejudice the rights of 'existing non-Jewish communities' - about 90% of the population, and not named.
events.significance: One sentence in a private letter became an article of international law when it was written into the Mandate for Palestine in 1922. It committed Britain to a project that could not be reconciled with what it had told Sharif Hussein in 1915, and it is the document from which the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's legal history begins.

places.name: Foreign Office, Whitehall, London
places.note: Where the letter was drafted and redrafted through 1917.

people.name: Arthur Balfour
people.role: Foreign Secretary who signed the letter

people.name: Chaim Weizmann
people.role: chemist and Zionist leader whose lobbying secured the declaration

people.name: Edwin Montagu
people.role: Secretary of State for India and the only Jewish member of the cabinet, who opposed the declaration as antisemitic in effect

people.name: Walter Rothschild
people.role: the letter's addressee, as a leader of the British Jewish community

pedagogy.hook: The Balfour Declaration is 67 words long and does not contain the word 'Arab' - it calls 90% of Palestine's population 'existing non-Jewish communities'.

misconception.belief: The Balfour Declaration promised a Jewish state.
misconception.correction: It said 'a national home', a phrase chosen because it was undefined; it also said nothing should prejudice the rights of the existing population, and nothing should prejudice the status of Jews in other countries. Every party read it differently, which was partly the point at the time and entirely the problem afterwards.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how a wartime diplomatic manoeuvre became binding law, and how the wording of a single sentence can shape a century.

evidence.author: Tom Segev
evidence.work: One Palestine, Complete: Jews and Arabs under the British Mandate
evidence.supports: The drafting of the declaration and its reception in Palestine.

evidence.author: Rashid Khalidi
evidence.work: The Iron Cage: The Story of the Palestinian Struggle for Statehood
evidence.supports: The declaration's effect on Palestinian political prospects.

contested.note: Historians disagree about why Britain issued it: to win American and Russian Jewish support for the war, to secure a friendly presence beside the Suez Canal, out of Christian Zionist conviction, or all three. The motive is argued; the text is not.

events.title: The Iraqi revolt of 1920
events.summary: When the San Remo mandate became known, the confederations of the mid-Euphrates rose against British rule, backed by a fatwa from the Shia marja Muhammad Taqi al-Shirazi and joined by Sunni officers and Baghdad nationalists. Britain needed about 100,000 troops, five months and £40 million to put it down.
events.significance: The revolt convinced London that direct rule in Iraq was unaffordable. Within a year Britain had installed a king, invented an Iraqi state and switched to policing the country from the air - the model of indirect control that shaped the whole interwar Middle East.

places.name: Najaf
places.note: Where al-Shirazi issued the fatwa declaring British rule unlawful.

places.name: Rumaytha
places.note: Where the rising began at the end of June 1920.

people.name: Muhammad Taqi al-Shirazi
people.role: Shia marja in Karbala whose fatwa lit the revolt; died in August 1920

people.name: Dhari al-Mahmud
people.role: Zoba sheikh whose followers killed Colonel Gerard Leachman at Fallujah in August 1920

people.name: Arnold Wilson
people.role: acting Civil Commissioner whose refusal of Iraqi self-government helped provoke the rising; replaced in October 1920

people.name: Gertrude Bell
people.role: Oriental Secretary who reported the revolt to London and then helped design the monarchy that followed

toll.money: The suppression cost Britain about £40 million, more than it had spent on the whole Arab Revolt, at a moment when the Treasury was cutting everything.
toll.note: Iraqi dead are usually given as 6,000 to 10,000; British and Indian dead as about 500. The Iraqi figure comes from British estimates and later Iraqi accounts and has never been independently established.

pedagogy.hook: The 1920 revolt is the one time in modern Iraqi history that Sunni and Shia rose together, and it happened against Britain.

misconception.belief: Sunni and Shia in Iraq have always been divided.
misconception.correction: In 1920 they were not: the fatwa came from Najaf and Karbala, the Baghdad organisers were Sunni, and mosques held joint gatherings. The sectarian shape of Iraqi politics owes a great deal to what Britain built afterwards - a Sunni monarchy and officer corps over a Shia majority.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment Britain chose indirect rule and air power over administration, a choice that echoed through Iraq for the next forty years.

evidence.author: Charles Tripp
evidence.work: A History of Iraq
evidence.supports: The revolt, its composition and its consequences.

evidence.author: Toby Dodge
evidence.work: Inventing Iraq: The Failure of Nation Building and a History Denied
evidence.supports: The turn to air control and indirect rule after 1920.

events.title: The Cairo Conference
events.summary: Winston Churchill gathered about forty British officials at the Semiramis Hotel in Cairo and in twelve days settled the Middle East on the cheap: Faisal for the throne of Iraq, Abdullah for Transjordan, the RAF to police both, and the garrison bill cut from £30 million to under £10 million a year.
events.significance: Two countries and two dynasties were decided in under a fortnight by people who were not from either. Jordan still has the family chosen there; Iraq had it until 1958. The conference is the clearest single instance of the empire making states to fit a budget.

places.name: Semiramis Hotel, Cairo
places.note: Where the conference sat from 12 to 30 March 1921.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where Churchill met Abdullah at the end of March and offered him Transjordan.

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: Colonial Secretary who convened the conference and took its decisions

people.name: Gertrude Bell
people.role: the only woman with executive authority present; argued for Faisal and drew much of Iraq's political shape

people.name: T. E. Lawrence
people.role: adviser on Arab affairs; regarded the settlement as partial payment of Britain's debt to the Hashemites

people.name: Percy Cox
people.role: High Commissioner for Iraq, who executed the plan and ran Faisal's plebiscite

people.name: Hugh Trenchard
people.role: Chief of the Air Staff, whose air-control scheme made the savings possible

toll.money: Britain's Middle East garrison bill fell from roughly £30 million a year to under £10 million within two years - the conference's real purpose.
toll.note: The saving was achieved by replacing infantry with aircraft, which meant bombing villages instead of occupying them.

pedagogy.hook: Two countries and two royal families were decided in twelve days at a Cairo hotel by about forty British officials, mainly to save money.

misconception.belief: Britain and France carefully designed the modern Middle East at the Paris peace conference.
misconception.correction: Much of it was improvised afterwards, under budget pressure. Cairo in March 1921 settled Iraq's king, Transjordan's emir and the RAF's role in both, and the driving argument in the room was the cost of the garrisons.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the mechanism by which states were made: not a grand plan but a series of expedient deals, whose consequences outlived everyone in the room.

evidence.author: John Darwin
evidence.work: Britain, Egypt and the Middle East: Imperial Policy in the Aftermath of War 1918-1922
evidence.supports: The financial pressures and the Cairo settlement.

evidence.author: Peter Sluglett
evidence.work: Britain in Iraq: Contriving King and Country
evidence.supports: The decisions on Iraq and their implementation.

events.title: The Uqair Protocol
events.summary: At a tented conference on the Gulf coast, Sir Percy Cox lost patience with five days of argument, took a map and drew the borders between Nejd, Iraq and Kuwait himself. Kuwait lost roughly two thirds of the territory it claimed; two Neutral Zones were invented where nobody could agree.
events.significance: These are the lines that still separate Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait. They cut across grazing routes held in common for centuries, gave Iraq only 58 kilometres of coast, and left the Kuwaiti border ambiguous enough to be cited by Baghdad in 1961 and 1990.

places.name: Uqair
places.note: A small port on the Hasa coast where the conference met in November and December 1922.

people.name: Percy Cox
people.role: High Commissioner for Iraq; drew the lines himself when the parties would not agree

people.name: Abdulaziz ibn Saud
people.role: Emir of Nejd, who gained most of the disputed ground

people.name: Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah
people.role: Sheikh of Kuwait, who was not at the conference and lost two thirds of his claim

people.name: Harry St John Philby
people.role: British adviser to Ibn Saud, present at Uqair

pedagogy.hook: Kuwait lost two thirds of its territory at a conference it did not attend, because a British official got tired of arguing and drew the line himself.

misconception.belief: Middle Eastern borders follow tribes, rivers or old provinces.
misconception.correction: Many follow the temper and the pencil of a British official on a particular afternoon. Uqair fixed the Saudi, Iraqi and Kuwaiti borders in 1922, cut across grazing routes the Bedouin had used for centuries, and invented two Neutral Zones because nobody could agree who owned the wells.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Gulf War of 1990-91 was fought partly over a line drawn at Uqair in 1922 by a man who had never been asked to draw it.

evidence.author: Gary Troeller
evidence.work: The Birth of Saudi Arabia: Britain and the Rise of the House of Sa'ud
evidence.supports: The Uqair conference and the boundary settlement.

evidence.author: Simon C. Smith
evidence.work: Britain's Revival and Fall in the Gulf: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, and the Trucial States, 1950-71
evidence.supports: The later consequences of the Kuwaiti boundary.

contested.note: The vivid story of Cox drawing the line on the map in front of the delegates comes largely from the memoir of his secretary, Harold Dickson, and is repeated everywhere. The boundaries and the outcome are documented; the theatre of the moment rests on one witness.

events.title: The Arab Revolt in Palestine
events.summary: Palestinian Arabs began a general strike in April 1936 demanding an end to Jewish immigration and land sales and a national government; it became a three-year rural insurgency. Britain deployed some 25,000 troops, demolished about 2,000 houses, hanged 108 people and dynamited much of old Jaffa.
events.significance: The revolt broke Palestinian Arab political and military capacity a decade before 1948, and it produced the 1939 White Paper capping Jewish immigration at 75,000 - which in turn produced the Jewish insurgency against Britain. Both communities' wars with Britain begin here.

places.name: Jaffa
places.note: Where the strike began and where the army demolished hundreds of houses in June 1936 to open 'roads'.

places.name: Jenin
places.note: Centre of the rural insurgency; part of the town was demolished in reprisal in August 1938.

people.name: Izz ad-Din al-Qassam
people.role: preacher whose killing by police in November 1935 helped ignite the revolt; his name was later taken by Hamas's armed wing

people.name: Amin al-Husayni
people.role: Mufti of Jerusalem and chairman of the Arab Higher Committee; fled Palestine in October 1937

people.name: Abd al-Rahim al-Hajj Muhammad
people.role: the revolt's most effective field commander; killed in March 1939

people.name: Charles Tegart
people.role: police adviser who built the fortified police stations and the northern border fence, and introduced interrogation methods later condemned

people.name: Orde Wingate
people.role: British officer who formed the Special Night Squads with Haganah members, training tactics used again in 1948

toll.note: Matthew Hughes (2019) gives roughly 5,000 Palestinian Arab dead, about 400 Jews and 262 British. Some estimates of Arab dead run higher; over 10% of the adult male Arab population was killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled. Around 2,000 houses were demolished as collective punishment.

pedagogy.hook: Britain hanged 108 people and demolished about 2,000 houses in Palestine between 1936 and 1939, and by the end the Palestinian national movement had lost its leaders, its weapons and its organisation.

misconception.belief: Palestinians did nothing until 1948 and then simply left.
misconception.correction: They fought a three-year national revolt from 1936 to 1939 and were defeated by the British Army. By 1948 their leadership was exiled or dead, their fighters disarmed and their villages already surveyed. The 1936-39 defeat is a large part of the explanation for 1948.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest example of British counter-insurgency in the Middle East, and the methods - collective punishment, house demolition, fortified police posts, night squads - were carried into later conflicts by the men Britain trained in them and by the states that came after.

evidence.author: Matthew Hughes
evidence.work: Britain's Pacification of Palestine: The British Army, the Colonial State, and the Arab Revolt, 1936-1939
evidence.supports: The military campaign, the methods used and the casualty figures.

evidence.author: Rashid Khalidi
evidence.work: The Iron Cage: The Story of the Palestinian Struggle for Statehood
evidence.supports: The revolt's effect on Palestinian political capacity.

events.title: The UN partition plan for Palestine
events.summary: The UN General Assembly voted 33 to 13, with 10 abstentions, to divide Palestine into a Jewish state on about 56% of the land, an Arab state on about 43%, and an international zone around Jerusalem. Britain, which had referred the question to the UN in April, abstained and refused to help implement the result.
events.significance: It is the legal origin of the State of Israel and the moment the Palestinian Arab case moved from a British argument to an international one. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan; the Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it as an award of most of the country to a third of the population.

places.name: Flushing Meadows, New York
places.note: Where the General Assembly sat in November 1947.

people.name: Ernest Bevin
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who referred Palestine to the UN and then refused to enforce its decision

people.name: David Ben-Gurion
people.role: chairman of the Jewish Agency; accepted partition as a basis and prepared for the war he expected

people.name: Jamal al-Husayni
people.role: acting chairman of the Arab Higher Committee, who argued at the UN that partition awarded most of the country to a minority

people.name: Ralph Bunche
people.role: UN official who drafted much of the partition scheme and later mediated the 1949 armistices

pedagogy.hook: Britain put Palestine to the United Nations, watched the vote, abstained, and then announced it would not lift a finger to carry out the result.

misconception.belief: The UN created Israel and Britain implemented the plan.
misconception.correction: The UN recommended partition; a General Assembly resolution is not binding. Britain refused to implement it, blocked the UN commission from entering Palestine, and simply left on 14 May 1948. The state that emerged was made by a war fought after Britain had gone.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a rare, dateable moment when an imperial power handed a problem it had created to an international body and walked away.

evidence.author: Wm. Roger Louis
evidence.work: The British Empire in the Middle East, 1945-1951: Arab Nationalism, the United States, and Postwar Imperialism
evidence.supports: Britain's referral to the UN and its refusal to implement partition.

evidence.author: Benny Morris
evidence.work: The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited
evidence.supports: The war that followed the vote.

events.title: The end of the Palestine Mandate
events.summary: At midnight on 14 May 1948 the British Mandate for Palestine expired. The High Commissioner had already sailed from Haifa, Israel had been declared in Tel Aviv that afternoon, and five Arab armies crossed the frontiers within hours. Britain transferred authority to nobody.
events.significance: It is the only case in the empire's history where Britain left a territory without arranging a successor government of any kind. The war that followed established Israel, destroyed the proposed Arab state, and made roughly 700,000 Palestinians refugees.

places.name: Haifa
places.note: Where the last High Commissioner boarded a cruiser on 14 May 1948.

places.name: Tel Aviv
places.note: Where Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel on the afternoon of 14 May.

people.name: Alan Cunningham
people.role: last High Commissioner for Palestine

people.name: David Ben-Gurion
people.role: declared the State of Israel and led it through the war

people.name: John Bagot Glubb
people.role: British commander of Jordan's Arab Legion, which fought Israeli forces in Jerusalem while Britain officially stood aside

toll.note: About 6,000 Israelis died, roughly 1% of the Jewish population, and an estimated 8,000 to 15,000 Arabs. The number of Palestinians displaced is usually given as 700,000 to 750,000, and UN estimates at the time were about 720,000. Over 400 villages were depopulated.

pedagogy.hook: Britain ended thirty years of rule in Palestine by naming a date, packing up, and handing power to nobody at all.

misconception.belief: Empires always handed over to a successor government.
misconception.correction: Palestine is the counter-example. There was no independence ceremony, no transfer of the seal, no successor administration. The High Commissioner left, the mandate lapsed at midnight, and the question of who governed was settled by a war.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the sharpest test of the claim that British decolonisation was orderly and planned.

evidence.author: Benny Morris
evidence.work: The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited
evidence.supports: The war of 1947-49 and the displacement.

evidence.author: Tom Segev
evidence.work: One Palestine, Complete: Jews and Arabs under the British Mandate
evidence.supports: The end of the mandate and the British departure.

contested.note: The causes of Palestinian displacement in 1948 are argued: flight from fighting, orders from Arab commanders in some places, and expulsion by Israeli forces in others. Benny Morris's archival work established that expulsions were widespread while rejecting the claim of a single master plan; other historians read the same evidence more strongly in either direction.

events.title: Abadan and the 1953 coup in Iran
events.summary: Iran nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which had paid the British Treasury more in tax in 1950 than it paid Iran in royalties. Britain evacuated Abadan, the largest refinery in the world, blockaded Iranian oil, and when that failed persuaded Washington to help overthrow Mohammad Mossadegh.
events.significance: It was the last time Britain tried to reverse a nationalisation in the Middle East by force and the first time it needed the Americans to do it. The 1954 consortium ended the British oil monopoly, and the coup is remembered in Iran as the reason a revolution in 1979 was aimed at foreign influence as much as at the Shah.

places.name: Abadan refinery
places.note: The largest oil refinery in the world; British staff left in October 1951.

places.name: Tehran
places.note: Where the coup of 19 August 1953 took place.

people.name: Mohammad Mossadegh
people.role: prime minister who nationalised the oil industry; overthrown and held under house arrest until his death

people.name: Christopher Woodhouse
people.role: British intelligence officer who sold the coup plan to Washington after Britain was expelled from Iran

people.name: Kermit Roosevelt Jr
people.role: CIA officer who directed the coup on the ground

people.name: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
people.role: Shah, who fled to Rome and returned three days later

toll.money: In 1950 the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company paid about £50 million in UK tax and around £16 million to Iran in royalties. Iran's share of the profits was a fraction of what American companies were paying Saudi Arabia under the 50-50 deal of 1950.
toll.note: Deaths in the Tehran street fighting of 19 August 1953 are usually put at 200 to 300. Britain denied involvement for sixty years; the CIA acknowledged its own role in 2013.

pedagogy.hook: In 1950 an oil company paid the British government three times more in tax than it paid Iran for Iran's oil. When Iran objected, Britain helped overthrow the government that said so.

misconception.belief: The 1953 coup was an American Cold War operation.
misconception.correction: It began as a British operation about oil. Britain was expelled from Iran in 1952 and took the plan to Washington, where it was resold as anti-communism. Both governments participated; the initiative and the grievance were British.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows informal empire in action after formal empire had gone, and its consequences are still visible in Iranian politics.

evidence.author: Ervand Abrahamian
evidence.work: The Coup: 1953, the CIA, and the Roots of Modern U.S.-Iranian Relations
evidence.supports: The oil dispute, the British initiative and the coup.

evidence.author: Nikki R. Keddie
evidence.work: Modern Iran: Roots and Results of Revolution
evidence.supports: The nationalisation crisis in Iranian politics.

events.title: The Jebel Akhdar war in Oman
events.summary: The elected Imam of Oman's interior, Ghalib bin Ali, and his brother Talib fought the Sultan of Muscat, whom Britain backed. The RAF bombed forts, villages, water channels and crops from Sharjah and Bahrain, and in January 1959 the SAS climbed the Jebel Akhdar plateau at night and ended the revolt.
events.significance: Britain fought a war in a country it insisted was not a British possession, for a sultan who ruled a state Britain said was independent, largely because oil concessions in the interior depended on the sultan's writ running there. It is the sharpest illustration of what informal empire could mean.

places.name: Jebel Akhdar
places.note: A plateau 2,000 metres up, taken by the SAS in January 1959.

places.name: Nizwa
places.note: The Imamate's capital, taken by Sultan's forces with British support in 1955 and 1957.

people.name: Ghalib bin Ali al-Hinai
people.role: elected Imam of Oman; exiled to Saudi Arabia and campaigned at the UN for twenty years

people.name: Talib bin Ali al-Hinai
people.role: the Imam's brother and military commander on the Jebel

people.name: Suleiman bin Hamyar
people.role: lord of the Jebel Akhdar who joined the revolt

people.name: Said bin Taimur
people.role: Sultan of Muscat and Oman, whose authority Britain restored

people.name: David Smiley
people.role: seconded British officer commanding the Sultan's Armed Forces

toll.note: There is no reliable death toll. British casualties were light; Omani losses among the rebels and in the bombed villages were never counted. RAF records show over a thousand sorties and the deliberate destruction of falaj irrigation channels and crops, which caused hunger rather than immediate deaths.

pedagogy.hook: Britain bombed villages in Oman for two years to keep a sultan on his throne in a country Britain officially said was not part of its empire.

misconception.belief: Britain's imperial wars ended with the Second World War and decolonisation.
misconception.correction: Between 1945 and 1976 Britain fought in Palestine, Malaya, Kenya, Cyprus, Suez, Oman twice, Aden, Borneo and Dhofar. The Oman campaigns are the least known because Britain denied at the time that it was fighting a war at all - questions in the Commons were answered by saying that these were the Sultan's operations.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows a war fought for oil concessions in a place with no British flag, and it explains why Oman had a British-commanded army into the 1980s.

evidence.author: J. E. Peterson
evidence.work: Oman's Insurgencies: The Sultanate's Struggle for Supremacy
evidence.supports: The Imamate revolt and the campaigns of 1955-59.

events.title: The Federation of South Arabia
events.summary: Britain merged six of the protectorate sultanates into a federation in 1962 and then, on 18 January 1963, pushed the Colony of Aden into it against the wishes of Aden's trade unions and much of its legislature, hoping conservative rulers would outvote the port's radical politics.
events.significance: It was the plan that produced the insurgency. Aden's unionised, literate, largely Yemeni-migrant workforce was locked into a federation of hereditary rulers with no vote in the matter, and within nine months the Aden Emergency had begun.

places.name: Al-Ittihad
places.note: The purpose-built federal capital outside Aden, now Madinat ash-Sha'b.

people.name: Abdullah al-Asnag
people.role: secretary-general of the Aden Trades Union Congress; led the opposition to the merger

people.name: Duncan Sandys
people.role: Colonial Secretary who pushed the merger through

people.name: Kennedy Trevaskis
people.role: British High Commissioner and architect of the federation

toll.note: No direct casualties. The federation's creation is counted here as a political cause of the war that followed, not as a violent event in itself.

pedagogy.hook: Britain put the most politically organised port in Arabia into a federation of hereditary sultans and hoped the sultans would outvote the dockers.

misconception.belief: Britain's federations were about preparing colonies for independence.
misconception.correction: They were usually about managing costs and diluting opposition. South Arabia in 1963, like Central Africa in 1953 and the West Indies in 1958, merged units with incompatible politics to produce a manageable successor. All three collapsed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the decision that turned a colonial port into a war, and it was taken by people in London who thought Aden's electorate was the problem.

evidence.author: Spencer Mawby
evidence.work: British Policy in Aden and the Protectorates 1955-67: Last Outpost of a Middle East Empire
evidence.supports: The design and consequences of the federation.

events.title: The Aden Emergency
events.summary: Fighting began in the Radfan mountains in October 1963 and a grenade was thrown at the High Commissioner at Aden airport in December; Britain declared an emergency. Four years of mountain campaigns, urban bombings and internment ended with British troops flying out on 29 November 1967.
events.significance: Aden was Britain's most complete defeat of the decolonisation era: no negotiated constitution, no chosen successor, no ceremony. The federation collapsed, the rulers Britain had subsidised for eighty years fled, and the National Liberation Front took power by force.

places.name: Crater, Aden
places.note: Retaken by the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders on 3-4 July 1967 after 22 British soldiers were killed on 20 June.

places.name: Radfan
places.note: Mountain district north of Aden where the fighting began in October 1963.

people.name: Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi
people.role: NLF secretary-general and first president of South Yemen

people.name: Abdullah al-Asnag
people.role: trade union leader and FLOSY politician, on the losing side of the NLF-FLOSY war

people.name: Humphrey Trevelyan
people.role: last High Commissioner, sent to organise the evacuation

people.name: Colin Mitchell
people.role: commanded the recapture of Crater in July 1967

people.name: Rajab Abdullah
people.role: Qutaybi leader in the Radfan in the first phase of the revolt

toll.note: British service deaths are usually given as about 90 to 130 in Aden and Radfan. Several hundred civilians were killed by bombs and shootings on all sides, and hundreds more died in the NLF-FLOSY fighting of 1967. No agreed total exists; the local dead were never systematically counted, which is itself part of the record.

pedagogy.hook: Britain left Aden without handing power to anyone: the last troops flew out on 29 November 1967 and the guerrillas who had beaten them declared a state the next day.

misconception.belief: Britain decided when and how to leave its colonies.
misconception.correction: In Aden it was pushed out. There was no negotiated constitution, no elected successor, no flag ceremony with a new prime minister. Britain talked to the NLF in Geneva only after the NLF had already taken control on the ground, and left before the new state was proclaimed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Aden is the counter-example to the story of orderly British withdrawal, and it happened in living memory to a colony Britain had held for 128 years.

evidence.author: Jonathan Walker
evidence.work: Aden Insurgency: The Savage War in South Arabia 1962-1967
evidence.supports: The military course of the emergency.

evidence.author: Spencer Mawby
evidence.work: British Policy in Aden and the Protectorates 1955-67: Last Outpost of a Middle East Empire
evidence.supports: The political collapse and the withdrawal decision.

contested.note: Casualty figures for the Aden Emergency vary widely between accounts and no authoritative total exists, particularly for Yemeni civilian and combatant dead. Allegations of torture at British interrogation centres, raised by Amnesty International in 1966 and examined by the Bowen inquiry, remain disputed in detail and largely accepted in outline.

events.title: The Dhofar rebellion
events.summary: A revolt in Oman's southern province, at first for local grievances and after 1968 under an avowedly Marxist front backed from South Yemen, was defeated over eleven years by the Sultan's forces under seconded British officers, with the SAS, Iranian troops and Jordanian engineers.
events.significance: It was Britain's longest post-imperial campaign in Arabia and the reason Britain helped depose Sultan Said bin Taimur in 1970: his refusal to spend money on schools, clinics or roads was recruiting for the rebels. The war ended the last serious challenge to the Gulf order Britain had built.

places.name: Salalah
places.note: Provincial capital and RAF staging base, defended through the war.

places.name: Mirbat

people.role: installed as sultan in July 1970 with British help; won the war by spending on development as well as fighting

people.name: Said bin Taimur

toll.note: There is no agreed total. Estimates of dead run from about 2,000 to 10,000 across eleven years; roughly 10,000 people fled into South Yemen. The Sultanate's figures and the Front's are both propaganda-adjacent, and no census-based study exists.

pedagogy.hook: Britain helped depose a sultan in 1970 because his refusal to build schools and clinics was recruiting for the guerrillas fighting him.

misconception.belief: Counter-insurgency is about military force.
misconception.correction: Dhofar is the campaign British officers cite to argue the opposite: wells, clinics, schools, an amnesty and a militia of former rebels mattered more than firepower. It is also worth noticing that Britain had spent forty years backing the ruler whose policies caused the war.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the last British war in Arabia, fought after every formal possession in the region had gone, and it shows how long informal empire outlived the map.

evidence.supports: The revolution, its politics and the British role.

events.title: The East of Suez decision
events.summary: Two months after devaluing the pound, Harold Wilson told the Commons that Britain would withdraw its forces from the Persian Gulf, Malaysia and Singapore by the end of 1971. The Gulf rulers, including Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi, offered to pay the full cost of keeping the British forces there. Britain refused.
events.significance: It ended 151 years of British military presence in the Gulf and forced nine sheikhdoms to invent a future in three years: Bahrain and Qatar chose independence, six emirates federated as the UAE, and Britain's world role shrank to Europe and the North Atlantic.

places.name: House of Commons, London
places.note: Where Wilson made the statement on 16 January 1968.

places.name: HMS Jufair, Bahrain
places.note: The Royal Navy base in Bahrain, closed in 1971 and now the site of the US Fifth Fleet headquarters.

people.name: Harold Wilson
people.role: prime minister who announced the withdrawal

people.name: Denis Healey
people.role: Defence Secretary who carried out the cuts

people.name: Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan
people.role: ruler of Abu Dhabi, who offered to pay for the British forces to stay and was turned down

people.name: William Luce
people.role: sent back to the Gulf in 1970 to negotiate a federation before the deadline

toll.money: The withdrawal was expected to save about £300 million a year by the mid-1970s. Britain's Gulf commitment cost roughly £12 million a year at the time - a sum the rulers offered to cover in full.
toll.note: The cost figures come from Treasury and Defence estimates of the period and were contested even then.

pedagogy.hook: When Britain announced it was leaving the Gulf, the Gulf rulers offered to pay the entire bill for the British forces to stay. Britain said no.

misconception.belief: Britain left its empire because colonised people demanded it, or because it believed in self-determination.
misconception.correction: In the Gulf there was no independence movement to speak of and the rulers wanted Britain to remain. Britain left because sterling was in crisis and the Labour cabinet needed cuts. Money decided this one, and the refusal of the rulers' offer proves it was about status and overstretch, not cash alone.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cleanest example in the whole atlas of empire ending for the metropole's reasons, on the metropole's timetable, against the wishes of the people being left.

events.title: The removal of the Chagossians

date.note: The removal was carried out in stages: people away in Mauritius were refused return from 1967, Diego Garcia was cleared in 1971, and the last families left Peros Banhos in May 1973. No single date exists.

events.summary: To make Diego Garcia available to the American military, Britain removed the whole population of the Chagos Archipelago between 1967 and 1973: people visiting Mauritius were refused return, supplies were cut off, about 800 pet dogs were gassed in a copra shed, and the last families were shipped out.
events.significance: It is the only case in which Britain deliberately depopulated a whole inhabited territory in the era of decolonisation, and it was done by an immigration ordinance in a colony created for the purpose. British courts found it unlawful in 2000; the International Court of Justice found the whole detachment unlawful in 2019.

places.name: Diego Garcia
places.note: Cleared in 1971; now a US airbase and naval support facility.

places.name: Peros Banhos
places.note: The last islands cleared, in May 1973.

places.name: Port Louis, Mauritius
places.note: Where most Chagossians were landed, many into destitution in the Cassis district.

people.name: Olivier Bancoult
people.role: leader of the Chagos Refugees Group and lead claimant in the British court cases

people.name: Marie Liseby Elyse

people.name: Denis Greenhill
people.role: Foreign Office official whose 1966 minute referred to the islanders as 'some few Tarzans or Man Fridays whose origins are obscure'

people.name: Bruce Greatbatch
people.role: BIOT Commissioner who ordered the killing of the islanders' dogs in 1971

toll.money: Britain paid Mauritius £650,000 in 1973 for the islanders' resettlement and £4 million in 1982 under a further agreement; much of it reached people late and in small amounts, and some signed away future claims with a thumbprint.
toll.note: The number removed is disputed because plantation records distinguished contract workers from long-settled families. The descendant community numbers roughly 10,000 today in Mauritius, Seychelles and the United Kingdom.

pedagogy.hook: Britain emptied an inhabited archipelago by refusing to let people who had gone to Mauritius for medical treatment sail home.

misconception.belief: The Chagos islands had no real population, only temporary contract workers.
misconception.correction: Families had lived there for five or six generations, with churches, schools, a hospital and graves. British officials described them in internal papers as 'Tarzans' and 'Man Fridays' precisely because their status as a settled people was inconvenient. The High Court in 2000 and the ICJ in 2019 both rejected the temporary-worker account.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest modern case of a British government acting against its own stated principles of self-determination, and the documents proving it were written by the officials who did it.

evidence.supports: The removal, the documents and the base.

events.title: The ICJ advisory opinion on the Chagos
events.summary: The International Court of Justice advised, by 13 votes to 1, that the 1965 detachment of the Chagos Archipelago was not a free expression of the Mauritian people's will, that decolonisation was therefore incomplete, and that Britain must end its administration as rapidly as possible.
events.significance: The world's highest court told a permanent member of the Security Council that it was running an unlawful colony in 2019. The UN General Assembly endorsed the opinion on 22 May 2019 by 116 votes to 6, and the finding led directly to the negotiations that produced the 2025 treaty.

places.name: Peace Palace, The Hague
places.note: Where the Court delivered the opinion.

people.name: Abdulqawi Yusuf
people.role: President of the International Court of Justice who delivered the opinion

people.name: Philippe Sands
people.role: counsel for Mauritius

people.name: Marie Liseby Elyse
people.role: Chagossian whose recorded statement was the only islander testimony before the Court

people.name: Olivier Bancoult
people.role: leader of the Chagos Refugees Group, present at the hearings

pedagogy.hook: In 2019 the International Court of Justice told Britain, by 13 votes to 1, that it was still running a colony unlawfully - and Britain said no.

misconception.belief: The age of empire is safely in the past and settled.
misconception.correction: It is being litigated now. The ICJ ruled in 2019, the UN General Assembly voted 116 to 6 in the same year, and Britain refused to comply until a treaty was signed in May 2025. This is the empire's last territorial dispute, and it is still moving.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows that the legal rules of decolonisation - that a colony must not be broken up before independence - were rules the empire itself had written and then broken.

evidence.author: Philippe Sands
evidence.work: The Last Colony: A Tale of Exile, Justice and Britain's Colonial Legacy
evidence.supports: The proceedings and the opinion.

evidence.author: Stephen Allen
evidence.work: The Chagos Islanders and International Law

events.title: The UK-Mauritius treaty on the Chagos
events.summary: The United Kingdom and Mauritius signed a treaty transferring sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago to Mauritius while leasing Diego Garcia back for the joint UK-US base for 99 years, with an annual payment to Mauritius and provision for Chagossians to resettle the outer islands.
events.significance: If it enters into force it ends the last territorial dispute of the British Empire in the Indian Ocean, sixty years after the archipelago was detached and six years after the International Court of Justice said the detachment was unlawful.

places.name: Diego Garcia
places.note: To be leased back to the UK for 99 years for the joint UK-US base.

people.name: Navin Ramgoolam
people.role: Prime Minister of Mauritius who signed the treaty; son of the premier who agreed the 1965 detachment

people.name: Olivier Bancoult
people.role: Chagossian leader; Chagossian groups were divided over whether the treaty served their community

evidence.author: Philippe Sands

evidence.supports: The legal and political road that led to the negotiations.

contested.note: This is the most recent event in the atlas and the most likely to have moved. The treaty was signed on 22 May 2025; entry into force depends on ratification and implementing legislation, and Chagossian organisations were publicly divided about it. Check the current legal position before stating that sovereignty has actually transferred.
